# C. Introduction

Studies and data relevant to key population and fishery processes are discussed below to provide background for the modeling choices made in this assessment. A model description is available on the github repository for GMACS and the files needed to reproduce these assessments also have a github repo, both of which are linked at the end of this document.

## Distribution
Snow crab (*Chionoecetes opilio*) are distributed on the continental shelf of the Bering Sea, Chukchi Sea, and in the western Atlantic Ocean as far south as Maine.  In the Bering Sea, snow crab are distributed widely over the shelf and are common at depths less than ~200 meters (see tech memo; Zacher et al., 2025). Smaller crab tend to occupy more inshore northern regions and mature crab occupy deeper areas to the south of the juveniles (see Zacher et al., 2025; Zheng et al. 2001). The eastern Bering Sea population within U.S. waters is managed as a single stock; however, the distribution of the population may extend into Russian waters to an unknown degree.

## Natural Mortality

Relatively few targeted studies exist to determine natural mortality for snow crab in the Bering Sea.  Nevissi, et al. (1995) used radiometric techniques to estimate shell age from last molt (Figure \@ref(fig:nevissi)).  The total sample size was 21 male crab (a combination of Tanner and snow crab) from a collection of 105 male crab from various hauls in the 1992 National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) Bering Sea survey. Representative samples for the 5 shell condition categories were collected from the available crab.  Shell condition 5 crab (SC5 = very, very old shell) had a maximum age of 6.85 years (s.d. 0.58, 95% CI approximately 5.69 to 8.01 years; carapace width of 110 mm).  The average age of 6 crab with SC4 (very old shell) and SC5, was 4.95 years (range: 2.70 to 6.85 years).  Given the small sample size, this maximum age may not represent the 1.5th percentile of the population that is approximately equivalent to Hoenig's method (1983). Tag recovery evidence from eastern Canada revealed observed maximum ages in exploited populations of 17-19 years (Nevissi, et al. 1995, Sainte-Marie 2002).  A maximum time at large of 11 years for tag returns of terminally molted mature male snow crab in the North Atlantic has been recorded since tagging started about 1993 (Fonseca, et al. 2008).  Fonseca, et al. (2008) estimated a maximum age of 7.8 years post terminal molt using data on dactyl wear.

```{r nevissi, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Radiometric estimates of shell age in male snow and Tanner crab collected during the NMFS survey of 1992. Reproduced from Ernst et al. (2005)'s presentation of Nevissi et al. (1995)."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/nevissi1.png")
```

In recent years, the mean for the prior for natural mortality used in the eastern Bering Sea snow crab assessment was based on the assumption that longevity would be at least 20 years in an unfished population of snow crab, informed by the studies above.  Under negative exponential depletion, the 99th percentile corresponding to age 20 of an unexploited population corresponds to a natural mortality rate of 0.23.  Using Hoenig's (1983) method a natural mortality equal to 0.23 corresponds to a maximum age of 18 years.

In contrast to the implied natural mortalities from the methodology used above, Murphy et al. (2018) estimated time-varying natural mortality for eastern Bering Sea snow crab with a mean of 0.49 for females and 0.36 for males based on the output of state-space models fit to NMFS survey data. Further, natural mortality estimates produced from empirical analyses by Then et al. (2015) and Hamel (2015) using similar assumed maximum ages as the methodology above produced natural mortalities larger than 0.23 (\autoref{natM_empir}). Then et al. (2015) compared several major empirical estimation methods for M (including Hoenig's method) with an updated data set and found that maximum age was the best available predictor. A maximum age of 20 years corresponded to an M of ~0.315 in Then et al.'s analysis. Hamel (2015) developed priors in a similar manner to Then et al., but forced the regression of observed natural mortality onto maximum age through the intercept, which resulted in an M of ~0.27 for an assumed maximum age of 20 years.

```{r,echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE,message=F}

# format all the above into a tabular format

dat<-data.frame( c(0.277,0.315,0.365),
            c(0.19,0.212,0.257),
            c(0.194, 0.223, 0.261),
            c(0.235, 0.271, 0.318))

rownames(dat)<-c(23,20,17)
colnames(dat)<-c("Then","Hoenig (1983)","Hoenig (2013)","Hamel")

pander(t(dat),split.cells=20,caption="\\label{natM_empir} Empirical estimates of natural mortality (per year) for a range of methods over a range of assumed maximum ages (column header). These are empirical estimators, not output of any assessment model.")

```

In addition to the results of empirical estimates of M from updated methodologies and state-space modeling by Murphy et al. (2018), inspection of the survey data suggests that natural mortality for mature individuals is higher than assumed. A fraction of the mature population (which are assumed not to grow, given evidence for a terminal molt) are not selected in the fishery (e.g. sizes 50-80 mm; Figure \@ref(fig:natm-mature)). Consequently, all mortality observed is 'natural'. The collapse in recruitment in the 1990s can be used as an instrument to understand natural mortality for mature individuals. The last large recruitment enters these size classes in the mid- to late-1990s and numbers of crab in these size classes return to low levels in less than 5 years.

```{r natm-mature, echo=FALSE, out.width="90%", fig.cap="Observed numbers at length of old-shell mature males by size class. The size bins presented are not vulnerable to the fishery, so all mortality observed in them is natural."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/old_shell_males_at_len.png")
```

The median value of the priors used in this assessment is set equal to values resulting from assuming a maximum age of 20 years and applying Hamel's methodology (0.271). A standard error of 0.0054 was used for initial priors and was estimated using the 95% CI of +-1.7 years on maximum age estimates from dactyl wear and tag return analysis in Fonseca, et al. (2008). Mortality events in 2018 and 2019 are estimated as additional mortality parameters applied by sex and maturity state to allow the model to fit recent population trends.

## Maturity

Maturity of females collected during the NMFS summer survey was determined by the shape of the abdomen, by the presence of brooded eggs, or egg remnants. Maturity for males was determined by chela height measurements, which were available most years starting from the 1989 survey (Otto 1998; Figure \@ref(fig:maturity-facet) & Figure \@ref(fig:maturity-facet-all)). Unless stated otherwise, mature male biomass means the biomass of morphometrically mature (large-clawed) males; the >= 95 mm and > 101 mm currencies are reported alongside it in Section F. A maturity curve for males was estimated using the average fraction mature based on chela height data and applied to years of survey data to estimate mature survey numbers that do not have chela height data available (see Richar and Foy, 2022 for details).

```{r maturity-facet, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Observed probability of having undergone terminal molt at size for new-shell male crab, based on chela height. Blue lines are earlier in the time series; red lines are the most recent."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/maturity_facet.png")
```

```{r maturity-facet-all, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Observed probability of having undergone terminal molt at size for new-shell male crab, based on chela height. The red line is the median over all years; blue lines are individual years."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/maturity_facet_all.png")
```

Bering Sea male snow crab appear to have a terminal molt to maturity based on hormone level data and findings from molt stage analysis via setagenesis (Tamone et al. 2005).  The models presented here assume a terminal molt for both males and females, which is supported by research on populations in the Bering Sea and the Atlantic Ocean (e.g. Dawe et al. 1991).

Mature male snow crab that do not molt may be important in reproduction.  Paul et al. (1995) found that old shell mature male Tanner crab out-competed new shell crab of the same size in breeding in a laboratory study.  Recently molted males did not breed even with no competition and may not breed until after ~100 days from molting (Paul et al. 1995).  Sainte-Marie et al. (2002) stated that only old shell males take part in mating for North Atlantic snow crab.

## Mating ratio and reproductive success

Bering Sea snow crab have historically been managed using morphometrically mature male biomass (MMB) as a proxy for reproductive potential. MMB is used as the currency for management because the fishery only retains large male crab, which are nearly 100% mature. Male snow crab are sperm conservers, using less than 4% of their sperm at each mating and females also can mate with more than one male. The amount of stored sperm and clutch fullness varies with sex ratio (Sainte-Marie 2002).  If mating with only one male is inadequate to fertilize a full clutch, then females would need to mate with more than one male, necessitating a sex ratio closer to 1:1 in the mature population, than if one male is assumed to be able to adequately fertilize multiple females. Although mature male biomass is currently the currency of management, some aspect of female reproduction is likely also an important indicator of reproductive potential of the stock.

 Clutch fullness is recorded for the females measured in the survey (see ESP; Fedewa et al., 2025). However, quantifying the reproductive potential of the female population from survey data can be difficult. For example, full clutches of unfertilized eggs may be extruded and appear normal to visual examination, and may be retained for several weeks or months by snow crab. Resorption of eggs may occur if not all eggs are extruded resulting in less than a full clutch.  Female snow crab at the time of the survey may have a full clutch of eggs that are unfertilized, resulting in overestimation of reproductive potential. Barren females may be a more obvious indication of low reproductive potential and increased in the early 1990s, decreased in the mid-1990s, then increased again in the late 1990s. The highest levels of barren females coincided with periods of high fishing mortality, but even then the proportion of barren females was low (see ESP; Fedewa et al., 2025). Biennial spawning is another confounding factor in determining the reproductive potential of snow crab. Laboratory analyses showed that female snow crab collected in waters colder than 1.5 degrees C from the Bering Sea spawn only every two years.

Further complicating the process of quantifying reproductive capacity, clutch fullness and fraction of unmated females may not account for the fraction of females that may have unfertilized eggs, since these cannot be detected by eye at the time of the survey.  The fraction of barren females observed in the survey may not be an accurate measure of fertilization success because females may retain unfertilized eggs for months after extrusion.  To examine this hypothesis, NMFS personnel sampled mature females from the Bering Sea in winter and held them in tanks until their eggs hatched in March of the same year (Rugolo et al. 2005).  All females then extruded a new clutch of eggs in the absence of males.  All eggs were retained until the crab were euthanized near the end of August.  Approximately 20% of the females had full clutches of unfertilized eggs.  The unfertilized eggs could not be distinguished from fertilized eggs by visual inspection at the time they were euthanized.  Indices of fertilized females based on the visual inspection method of assessing clutch fullness and percent unmated females may overestimate fertilized females.

## Growth

Several studies are available to estimate the growth per molt of male and female snow crab in the Bering Sea. These studies include:

1.  Transit study (2003); 14 crab
2.	Cooperative seasonality study; 6 crab
3.	Dutch Harbor holding study; 9 crab
4.	NMFS Kodiak holding study held less than 30 days;  6 crab
5.  NMFS Kodiak holding study 2016; 5 crab
6.  NMFS Kodiak holding study 2017; 70 crab.
7.  BSFRF/NMFS holding study 2018; 4 crab.
8.  BSFRF/NMFS holding study 2021; 177 crab.

In the "Transit study", pre- and post-molt measurements of 14 male crab that molted soon after being captured were collected.  The crab were measured when shells were still soft because all died after molting, so measurements may be underestimates of post-molt width (L. Rugolo, pers. com.). The holding studies include only data for crab held less than 30 days because growth of crab held until the next spring's molting was much lower. Crab missing more than two limbs were excluded due to other studies showing lower growth. Crab from the seasonal study were excluded that were measured less than 3 days after molting due to difficulty in measuring soft crab accurately (L. Rugolo, pers. comm.). In general, growth of snow crab in the Bering Sea appears to be greater than growth of some North Atlantic snow crab stocks (Sainte-Marie 1995).  Crab in their first few years of life may molt more than once per year, however, the smallest crab included in the model are approximately 4 years old and would be expected to molt annually.

## Management history

## ADF&G harvest strategy

Before the year 2000, the Guideline Harvest Level (GHL) for retained crab only was a 58% harvest rate of the number of male crab over 101 mm CW estimated from the survey.  The minimum legal size limit for snow crab is 78 mm, however, the snow crab market generally only accepts crab greater than 101 mm.  In 2000, due to the decline in abundance and the declaration of the stock as overfished, the harvest rate for calculation of the GHL was reduced to 20% of male crab over 101 mm.  After 2000, a rebuilding strategy was developed based on simulations by Zheng et al. (2002) using survey biomass estimates. The realized retained catch often exceeded the GHL historically.

The Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) harvest strategy since 2000 sets harvest rate based on estimated mature biomass. The harvest rate scales with the status of the population relative to a proxy for B~*MSY*~, which is calculated as the average total mature biomass at the time of the survey from 1983 to present and MSST is one half the B~*MSY*~ proxy.  The harvest rate begins at 0.10 when total mature biomass exceeds 50% MSST (230 million lbs) and increases linearly to 0.225 when biomass is equal to or greater than the B~*MSY*~ proxy (Zheng et al. 2002).

\begin{equation}
 u =
 \begin{cases}
 Bycatch  & if \frac{TMB}{TMB_{MSY}} \leq 0.25 \\[3ex]
 \frac {0.225 ( \frac {TMB}{TMB_{MSY}} - \alpha)}{1-\alpha}  & if 0.25 < \frac {TMB}{TMB_{MSY}} < 1 \\[3ex]
 0.225 & if TMB >TMB_{MSY}
\end{cases}
\end{equation}

Where *TMB* is the total mature biomass and TMB~*BMSY*~ is the *TMB* associated with maximum sustainable yield. The maximum retained catch is set as the product of the exploitation rate, *u*, calculated from the above control rule and survey mature male biomass.  If the retained catch in numbers is greater than 58% of the estimated number of new shell crab greater than 101 mm plus 25% of the old shell crab greater than 101 mm, the catch is capped at 58%.

## History of BMSY

Prior to adoption of Amendment 24, B~*MSY*~ was defined as the average total mature biomass (males and females) estimated from the survey for the years 1983 to 1997 (921.6 million lbs; NPFMC 1998) and MSST was defined as 50% of B~*MSY*~. Currently, the biological reference point for biomass is calculated using a spawning biomass per recruit proxy, B~*35%*~ (Clark, 1993). B~*35%*~ is the biomass at which spawning biomass per recruit is 35% of unfished levels and has been shown to provide close to maximum sustainable yield for a range of stock productivities (Clark, 1993). [[author: Clark (1993) is cited here but has no entry in Section K; the September 2025 assessment has the same gap. Supply the reference.]] Consequently, it is an often used target when a stock recruit relationship is unknown or unreliable.  The range of years of recruitment used to calculate biomass reference points is from 1982 to the present assessment year, minus 1. However, recent analyses suggest SPR-based reference points do not provide a meaningful constraint on the snow crab fishery when the probability of having undergone terminal molt is specified to reflect observations in the survey. This is because a large fraction of the population matures (and ceases growing) at a size smaller than is harvested by the fishery.

## Fishery history

Snow crab were harvested in the Bering Sea by the Japanese from the 1960s until 1980 when the Magnuson Act prohibited foreign fishing. After the closure to foreign fleets, retained catches increased from relatively low levels in the early 1980s (e.g.  `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1982)$obs[1]),2)` kt during 1982) to historical highs in the 1990s (retained catches during 1991, 1992, and 1998 were `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1991)$obs[1]),2)`, `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1992)$obs[1]),2)`, and `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1998)$obs[1]),2)` kt, respectively).  The stock was declared overfished in 1999 at which time retained catches dropped to levels similar to the early 1980s (e.g. `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==2000)$obs[1]),2)` kt). Retained catches slowly increased after 1999 before dropping again in 2016. Total allowable catches were reduced with the collapse of the population in 2021, the fishery was closed for the first time in 2022, and the closure continued through 2023. A small fishery occurred in 2024, with 2.15 kt retained, and a larger one in 2025, when the State set a total allowable catch of 4.22 kt and 4.13 kt was retained. <!-- TODO 2026: extend to the 2025/26 fishery once characterized (ADF&G retained ~4.1 kt in crab_year 2025). -->

Discard mortality from the directed fishery is the next largest source of mortality after retained catch and approximately tracks the retained catch. The highest estimated discard mortality occurred during 1990 at `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1990)$obs[2]),2)` kt which was `r round(100*as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1990)$obs[2])/ as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1990)$obs[1]),2)`% of the retained catch during that year. Discard mortality in 2024 was `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==2024)$obs[2]),2)` kt; the directed fishery was closed in 2022 and 2023, so no directed discards were recorded in those years. Non-directed mortality continues to be very small at `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==2024)$obs[4]),2)` kt in 2024.

Discards from the directed pot fishery have been estimated from observer data since 1992 and has ranged from 11-100% of the magnitude of retained catch by numbers. Discards reached 50-100% of the magnitude of retained catch in the lead up to the collapse after the 2018-2019 heatwave because of the large year class entering the population. Female discard catch has been very low compared to male discard catch and has not been a significant source of mortality. Discard mortality rates for the directed fishery are assumed to be 30%. Discard of snow crab in groundfish fisheries has been highest in the yellowfin sole trawl fishery, and decreases down through the flathead sole trawl fishery, Pacific cod bottom trawl fishery, rock sole trawl fishery, and the Pacific cod hook-and-line and pot fisheries, respectively (Figure \@ref(fig:bycatch)).  Bycatch in fisheries other than the groundfish trawl fishery has historically been relatively low. Discard mortality in the non-directed fisheries is taken as total in the models presented here: the trawl bycatch series enters the assessment with a discard mortality of 1, not the 0.8 applied when those removals are prepared. [[author: 01_prep_fishery_data.R applies 0.8 to trawl and 0.3 to other-crab bycatch before writing the series, and the model then applies 1 to it. Confirm that is intended and not a double or missing application.]] Size frequency data and catch per pot have been collected by observers on snow crab fishery vessels since 1992.  Observer coverage has been 10% on catcher vessels larger than 125 ft (since 2001), and 100% coverage on catcher processors (since 1992).

```{r bycatch, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Time series of non-directed bycatch from the groundfish fisheries by gear, in numbers of crab."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/bycatch.png")
```

Several modifications to pot gear have been introduced to reduce bycatch mortality.  In the 1978/79 season, escape panels were required on pots used in the snow crab fishery to prevent ghost fishing.  Escape panels consist of an opening with one-half the perimeter of the tunnel eye laced with untreated cotton twine.  The size of the cotton laced panel was increased in 1991 to at least 18 inches in length.  No escape mechanisms for undersized crab were required until the 1997 season when at least one-third of one vertical surface of pots had to contain not less than 5 inches stretched mesh webbing or have no less than four circular rings of no less than 3 3/4 inches inside diameter.  In the 2001 season the escapement provisions for undersized crab were increased to at least eight escape rings of no less than 4 inches placed within one mesh measurement from the bottom of the pot, with four escape rings on each side of the two sides of a four-sided pot, or one-half of one side of the pot must have a side panel composed of not less than 5 1/4 inch stretched mesh webbing.

# D. Data

Updated time series of survey indices and size compositions were calculated from data downloaded from the AKFIN database. Bycatch data (biomass and size composition) were updated for the most recent year from the AKFIN database. Retained, total, and discarded catch (in numbers and biomass) and size composition data for each of these data sources were updated for the most recent year based on files provided by the State of Alaska.

## Catch data

Catch data and size composition of retained crab from the directed snow crab pot fishery for crab years 1982 to 2025 were used in this analysis (Table \@ref(tab:obscatch)). Time series of discarded catch from the directed fishery are fit, but size composition data are for total catch. The discard male catch was estimated for crab years 1982 to 1991 in the model using the estimated fishery selectivities based on the observer data for crab years 1992 to 2025. The discards prior to 1992 may be underestimated due to the lack of escape mechanisms for undersized crab in the pots before 1997. See \autoref{datayears} for a summary of catch data range.

## Survey biomass and size composition data
Estimates of the numbers of crab by sex and size from the annual eastern Bering Sea (EBS) bottom trawl survey conducted by NMFS (e.g. Figure \@ref(fig:n-at-len) & Figure \@ref(fig:n-at-len-f); see Lang et al., 2018 for materials and methods; see the most recent tech memo for detailed description) are used to calculate the primary indices of abundance used in this assessment. Additional survey stations were added in 1989, which could alter the interpretation of the catchability coefficient for the survey. Consequently, survey selectivity has been historically modeled in two 'eras' in the assessment (1982-1988, 1989-present). All survey data in this assessment used measured net widths instead of the fixed 50 ft net width based on Chilton et al.'s (2009) survey estimates. Carapace width and shell conditions were measured and reported for snow crab caught in the survey.

```{r n-at-len, echo=FALSE, out.width="86%", fig.cap="Raw total numbers at size of male crab observed in the survey. Blue are all numbers at size; green are males > 101 mm carapace width, the industry-preferred size."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/size_bins_comp_Kodiak_m.png")
```

```{r n-at-len-f, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Raw total numbers at size of immature and mature female crab observed in the survey, binned at 5 mm intervals."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/n_at_l_f.png")
```

Mature male size composition data were calculated by multiplying the total numbers at length for new shell male crab by a vector of observed proportion of mature males at length. All old shell crab of both sexes were assumed to be mature.  New shell crab were demarcated as any crab with shell condition index <= 2. The biomass of new and old shell mature individuals was calculated by multiplying the vector of numbers at length by weight at length. These vectors were then summed by sex to provide the input for assessment (Table \@ref(tab:obsbio)).  Input sample sizes are specified as 100 for both sexes and maturity states for all years of survey size composition data.

```{r obsbio, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
## Observed survey biomass with its sampling CV -- a checklist requirement
## ("survey biomass estimates with measures of uncertainty") and the target of
## the obsbio reference, which pointed at a table in an eval = FALSE chunk until
## 2026-08-29. Read from the model's own input file, so the table cannot drift
## from what was fitted. 2020 is absent because the survey was cancelled.
##
## Each biomass carries its CV in the same cell, and the 44 survey years run in
## two blocks side by side. Kept apart and stacked, the table was ten columns
## and three pages, which both overflowed the line and made flextable repeat its
## caption and label on every continuation page (backlog 9b).
.si_path <- "data/derived/survey_indices.csv"
if (file.exists(.si_path)) {
  .si <- read.csv(.si_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  .cell <- function(b, cv) ifelse(is.na(b), "",
                                  sprintf("%.1f (%.2f)", b, cv))
  .mm <- .si[.si$sex == "male"   & .si$maturity == "mature", c("year","biomass","cv")]
  .mf <- .si[.si$sex == "female" & .si$maturity == "mature", c("year","biomass","cv")]
  .d  <- merge(.mm, .mf, by = "year", all = TRUE, suffixes = c(".m", ".f"))
  .d  <- .d[order(.d$year), ]
  stopifnot("survey_indices.csv should have no 2020 row (survey cancelled)" =
              !(2020 %in% .d$year))
  obsbio_df <- data.frame(
    Year   = as.character(.d$year),
    Male   = .cell(.d$biomass.m, .d$cv.m),
    Female = .cell(.d$biomass.f, .d$cv.f),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)

  .n <- nrow(obsbio_df); .half <- ceiling(.n / 2)
  .a <- obsbio_df[seq_len(.half), ]
  .b <- obsbio_df[seq.int(.half + 1L, .n), ]
  if (nrow(.b) < nrow(.a)) .b[seq.int(nrow(.b) + 1L, nrow(.a)), ] <- ""
  names(.b) <- paste0(names(.b), " ")
  obsbio_df <- cbind(.a, .b); rownames(obsbio_df) <- NULL

  flextable::flextable(obsbio_df) |>
    flextable::fontsize(size = 8, part = "all") |>
    flextable::align(j = 2:6, align = "right", part = "all") |>
    flextable::autofit() |>
    flextable::set_caption(
      caption = paste("Observed mature male and mature female biomass at the time of the",
                      "NMFS summer survey (1,000 t), each followed by the coefficient of",
                      "variation of that estimate in parentheses. These are the survey",
                      "observations fitted by every model presented. Years run down the",
                      "left block and continue in the right. There is no 2020 row: the",
                      "survey was cancelled that year."),
      autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "obsbio")
    )
}
```



## Spatial distribution of survey abundance and catch
Snow crab are distributed widely over the eastern Bering Sea shelf, but their density and the extent of their distribution have changed over time (see tech memo). Spatial gradients exist in the survey data by maturity and size for both sexes.  For example, larger males have been more prevalent on the southwest portion of the shelf while smaller males have been more prevalent on the northern portion of the shelf. Centroids of mature female abundance early in the history of the survey were farther south, but moved north during the 1990s. Since the late 1990s and early 2000s, the centroids moved south again, but not to the extent seen in the early 1980s. This phenomenon was mirrored in centroids of abundance for large males.

Fishing effort has generally been south of 58.5 N, even when ice cover did not restrict the fishery from moving farther north (Figure \@ref(fig:effort-sp) & Figure \@ref(fig:recent-eff)).  This is possibly due to the proximity to port and practical constraints of meeting delivery schedules. Unstandardized CPUE (hereafter just 'CPUE') in the fishery has varied over time and an increase in average CPUE occurred after rationalization (Figure \@ref(fig:year-cpue)).  The change in CPUE in a given spatial area within a season can reflect the impact of the fishery on the population in that area. Declines in CPUE can be seen by spatial area over time within a season (Figure \@ref(fig:cpue-trend)).

```{r effort-sp, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Distribution of effort, in pot lifts, in the directed fishery on the Bering Sea shelf, summed from 1990 to present. Squares are statistical areas defined by the State."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/aggregate_effort.png")
```

```{r recent-eff, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Yearly distribution of effort, in pot lifts, in the directed fishery on the Bering Sea shelf from 1990 to present. Only areas represented by three or more fishers and processors are shown."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/yearly_effort.png")
```

```{r year-cpue, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Yearly unstandardized catch per unit effort from 1990 to present, with the total number of crab captured (bottom)."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/timeseries_cpue.png")
```

```{r cpue-trend, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Trends in unstandardized CPUE by statistical area. Each line is a linear model fit through observed CPUE in a given area in a given year; trends were fit only where an area was represented by three or more fishers and processors."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/cpue_trend_area.png")
```

The observed distribution of large males during the summer survey and the fishery catch have historically differed, and the origin of this difference is unknown. It is possible that crab move between the fishery and the survey, but it is also possible that fishers do not target all portions of the distribution of large male crab equally. The underlying explanation of this phenomenon could hold implications for relative exploitation rates spatially and it has been suggested that high exploitation rates in the southern portion of the snow crab range may have resulted in a northward shift in snow crab distribution (Orensanz, 2004). Snow crab larvae likely drift north and east after hatching in spring. Snow crab appear to move south and west as they grow (Parada et al., 2010); however, little tagging data exists to fully characterize the ontogenetic or annual migration patterns of this stock (Murphy et al. 2010).

## Experimental study of survey selectivity

The Bering Sea Fisheries Research Foundation (BSFRF) has conducted supplementary surveys in the Bering Sea in which snow crab were caught during 2009, 2010, 2016, 2017, and 2018.  The location and extent of these surveys varied over the years as the survey goals changed. In 2009, the survey consisted of 108 tows around 27 survey stations and the goal was to improve understanding of snow crab densities and the selectivity of NMFS survey gear (Figure \@ref(fig:bsfrfmap)). Abundances estimated by the industry surveys were generally higher than the NMFS estimates, which suggests that the catchability of the NMFS survey gear is less than 1.

```{r bsfrfmap, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Location of the BSFRF survey selectivity experiments that provided data used in this assessment, over time."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/bsfrf_map.png")
```

In 2016, 2017, and 2018, snow crab were not the focus of the BSFRF surveys, but were still caught in the BSFRF gear. Comparing the ratio of the number of crab caught at length in the BSFRF gear (which is assumed to have a catchability/selectivity of 1 over all size classes) to the number of crab caught at length within the same area in the NMFS survey gear (which is assumed to have a catchability/selectivity <= to 1 for at least some of the size classes) can provide an empirical estimate of catchability/selectivity (Figure \@ref(fig:bsfrf-sel)). Empirical estimates of catchability/selectivity vary by year and size class across the different BSFRF data sets (Figure \@ref(fig:bsfrf-sel-all) & Figure \@ref(fig:emp-sel)). The number of snow crab used to develop estimates of numbers at length likely contributes to these differences among years (Figure \@ref(fig:bsfrf-sampn)), but other factors may also influence catchability/selectivity at size of the NMFS survey gear (e.g. Somerton et al. 2013 show substrate type can influence selectivity). GAMs fit to the empirical estimates of selectivity are used as priors on estimated selectivity in the currently used assessment model. The standard errors from the GAMs are input as weighting factors for each prior of selectivity at size and sex derived from the BSFRF data.

```{r bsfrf-sel, echo=FALSE, out.width="89%", fig.cap="Observed numbers at length extrapolated from length-composition data and estimates of total numbers within the survey selectivity experimental areas, by year (left), and the inferred selectivity, the ratio of crab at length in the NMFS gear to that in the BSFRF gear (right)."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/BSFRF_NMFS_select.png")
```

```{r bsfrf-sel-all, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Inferred survey selectivity for all available years of BSFRF data."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/BSFRF_NMFS_select_allyrs.png")
```

```{r emp-sel, echo=FALSE, out.width="64%", fig.cap="Inferred selectivity from the BSFRF experiments with selectivity at size class estimated by a generalized additive model (top), and by a sample-size-weighted average (bottom)."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/avg_BSFRF_sel_alt.jpg")
```

```{r bsfrf-sampn, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Number of crab collected in the BSFRF experimental areas by the NMFS survey and by the BSFRF survey."}
knitr::include_graphics("continuity/background/sample_sizes.png")
```

# E. Analytic approach


## Model description

The Generalized Model for Assessing Crustacean Stocks (GMACS) was adopted as the assessment platform for snow crab in 2022 after a demonstration that GMACS could effectively reproduce the dynamics of the status quo model and offered structural improvements. GMACS is an integrated, size-structured model developed using automatic differentiation software developed as a set of libraries under C++ (ADModel Builder).  ADModel Builder can estimate a large number of parameters in a non-linear model using automatic differentiation software extended from Griewank and Corliss (1991) and developed into C++ class libraries.  GMACS version 2.20.34 was used for the author-preferred software after the January 2026 CPT.

The snow crab population dynamics model tracks the number of crab of sex *s*,  maturity state *m*, during year *y* at width *w*, N~*s,m,y,w*~. A terminal molt was modeled in which crab move from an immature to a mature state, after which no further molting occurred. The mid-points of the size bins tracked in the model spanned from 27.5 to 132.5 mm carapace width, with 5 mm size classes. The number of estimated parameters differs among the models: 407 in `Model 25.3`, `Model 26.1` and `Model 26.1a`, 412 in `Model 26.1b`, 386 in `Model 26.1c`, and 234 in `Model 26.2`. Parameters estimated within the assessment included those associated with the population processes recruitment, growth, natural mortality (subject to an informative prior and two years of additional 'mortality events' estimated in 2018 and 2019), fishing mortality, selectivity (fisheries and survey), and catchability. The yearly probability of undergoing terminal molt, weight at size, discard mortality, bycatch mortality, variance in growth increment, and parameters associated with proportion of recruitment allocated to size bin were estimated outside of the model or specified. See the GMACS repo linked at the end of this document to peruse the control files that specify the population dynamics.

A lognormal distribution was assumed for all catch and index time-series, while a robust multinomial was assumed for all size composition data. No likelihood weights were used in the assessment.

A 'jittering' approach has been historically used to explore the impact of different starting values on the assessment output (Turnock, 2016). Parameter values were jittered based on a normal distribution centered on one with a standard deviation of `r jit_fmt(jit_sd, 2)` that was then translated to the parameter space defined by the initial value and its bounds. `r if (jit_have) sprintf("%s jitters were run for the author-recommended model (Table \\@ref(tab:model-overview)); each run was started from an independently perturbed parameter vector and re-fit to convergence.", jit_n)` Each jitter run used an explicitly recorded random seed, so the analysis is exactly reproducible; the seed used by every run is stored alongside its results. Four of the six models presented were jittered (Table \@ref(tab:model-overview)); `Model 25.3` and `Model 26.1a` were not.

## Model selection and evaluation
Models were evaluated based on their fit to the data, evidence of non-convergence, the credibility of the estimated population processes, and the strength of the influence of the assumptions of the model on the outcomes of the assessment. Note that for some of the model scenarios, data inputs are different and, therefore, model fits are not directly comparable.

### Model summaries

The key assumptions of these models include: 

* the probability of terminally molting at size varies over time and size and is specified as fixed inputs to the model based on observations from the survey data

* survey selectivity is estimated by era (1982-88; 1989-present) and sex as a non-parametric curve subject to priors based on the BSFRF survey efficiency experiment data

* growth is a linear function of pre-molt carapace width with a specified variability around post-molt size

* all immature crab molt

* natural mortality is estimated by sex and maturity state with additional mortality events estimated in 2018 and 2019 and subject to a prior based on an assumed longevity of 20 years

* total and retained fishery selectivity are estimated logistic curves

* all non-directed bycatch (e.g. snow crab caught in the Tanner crab fishery or crab caught in the non-pelagic trawl fisheries) is lumped into a single 'fishery' for which a single selectivity is estimated; these removals are recorded for both sexes combined, so in the male-only sensitivity they are fit by the male population alone and the bycatch fishing mortality estimated for males is correspondingly inflated (the affected removals average 0.48 kt against a mean retained catch of 37.1 kt, and the fit to the series is essentially unchanged)

* recruitment is estimated separately for females and males and is allocated in the first 3 size bins; the male-only sensitivity estimates male recruitment only


### Model scenarios

#### Model numbering and its correspondence with the May 2026 assessment {-}

The models presented here are numbered on the 2026 cycle, following the May 2026 Crab Plan Team report, which recorded that the 2025 accepted model had been mistakenly labeled `Model 25` in the preliminary assessment when its accepted number is `Model 25.3`, and that the runs introduced in May 2026 had been mistakenly numbered on the 2025 cycle rather than the 2026 one. The review guidelines distinguish major changes, which take a new integer, from minor ones, which take a letter; a change to the data alone is treated here as minor. Because the June 2026 SSC report refers to the configuration accepted in May by its May number, the correspondence is stated here in full.

| This document | May 2026 preliminary assessment | Terminal year | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model 25.3 | Model 25 | 2024 | 2025 accepted assessment, rolled forward |
| **Model 26.1** | **Model 25.2c** | 2024 | Configuration accepted by the CPT in May 2026 |
| Model 26.1a | Model 25.2e | 2024 | 26.1 with the binning and growth-data corrections |
| **Model 26.1b** | Model 25.2e (new data) | 2025 | **Author-recommended**; 26.1a with the 2025 fishery and 2026 survey |
| Model 26.1c | Model 25.2e (2019 data) | 2019 | 26.1b truncated to 2019, convergence diagnostic |
| Model 26.2 | Model 26.1 | 2025 | 26.1b with the female population removed |

The configuration the June 2026 SSC report calls `Model 25.2c` is `Model 26.1` in this document, and the author-recommended run, `Model 26.1b`, is that same configuration with the two data corrections and a further year of data.

#### The models {-}

A total of `r n_models` models were explored (Table \@ref(tab:model-overview)). All models share the same structural assumptions described above and differ only in the version of GMACS, their data inputs, the specification of the maturity ogive, and the definition of the plus group. The one exception is `Model 26.2`, which removes the female population entirely and is therefore a structural change. The naming convention reflects an additive series of changes layered onto the September 2025 model (`Model 25.3`). 

The base ('rolled forward') model:

* **Model 25.3** -- the September 2025 author-recommended model, included for reference only. No data are updated and no structural changes are made. It was fitted under an earlier version of GMACS and is reported as originally fitted.

Models carried forward from the May 2026 assessment:

* **Model 26.1** -- the model accepted by the CPT in May 2026. `Model 25.3` updated to GMACS 2.20.34, with the total-male size composition corrected and the plus group enlarged to include all crab greater than 135 mm carapace width, and with the molting probability controls replaced by the array produced by the new maturity workflow developed by the Kodiak lab (E. Ryznar, in prep). That workflow fits an `sdmTMB` spatiotemporal model to chela-based maturity classifications to produce a smoothed probability of being mature at size and location, integrated to a population-level annual ogive; the updated series shows a weaker temporal trend in the probability of terminal molt at intermediate sizes. Data end in 2024, as in May.

* **Model 26.1a** -- as `Model 26.1`, but with the size-composition bin convention changed so that a crab falling exactly on a 5 mm cutoff is assigned to the upper bin, and with a transcription error in the growth data corrected (a 26.3 mm crab's molt increment recorded as 73 mm where the specimen master gives 7.3 mm). Data end in 2024. Presented to isolate the effect of the two data corrections against the May baseline.

The September 2026 models:

* **Model 26.1b** -- the author-recommended model. The `Model 26.1a` configuration advanced to end year 2025, so that the fishery data run through the 2025/26 season and the survey data through the 2026 summer survey. The data change; the model does not.

* **Model 26.1c** -- the same configuration with all data truncated to 2019, so that the fishery data end with the 2019/20 season and the survey with the 2019 summer survey. Requested by the CPT in May 2026 to test whether the convergence problems originate in estimating recruitment following the 2018-19 collapse and across the 2020 survey gap. The estimated parameter count is 386.

Sensitivity to the female data and dynamics:

* **Model 26.2** -- `Model 26.1b` with the female population removed entirely rather than merely down-weighted. The number of sexes is set to one, which removes the female size compositions, the female survey indices, the female discard catch, and the female growth observations from the data, and removes the female recruitment, natural mortality, growth, and selectivity parameters from the model. The estimated parameter count falls from 412 to 234. Fixing the female estimation phases alone would not accomplish this: a combined-sex catch observation is predicted by summing over both sexes, and the recruitment scale and deviations are not sex-specific, so the female population would continue to influence fishing mortality and recruitment. The non-directed bycatch is recorded for both sexes combined and is therefore fit by the male population alone in this run, as noted among the assumptions above. This is the only model presented here that differs structurally from `Model 26.1a`, which is why it takes a new number rather than a parenthetical. Requested by the CPT in May 2026 and presented as a sensitivity only; like every other model here it is not proposed for the 2026/27 specification.

The May 2026 preliminary assessment presented a bracket of fourteen candidate models exploring three axes of uncertainty: the treatment of *Chionoecetes* hybrids, the new maturity workflow, and a set of attempts to improve convergence by correcting the total-male composition, expanding the plus group, and adding an immature survey index. That bracket is not repeated here. The CPT and SSC concluded that hybrid catch and survey data should not be included in the assessment model at this time, and agreed that the immature survey index should not be treated as a convergence fix, so neither the hybrid nor the immature-index candidates are carried forward. The composition correction and the expanded plus group, which the SSC supported as clear technical improvements, are incorporated in every model presented above. The full May bracket and its results remain available in the May 2026 preliminary assessment document.

Time series of data used in the assessment are visualized in Figures \@ref(fig:indexdataplots), \@ref(fig:catchdataplots) and \@ref(fig:compdataplots). [[author: if a survey-biomass comparison across the September models is wanted, add it here.]]

## Results
### Model convergence and comparison
The 2026 groundfish stock assessment guidelines set the convergence standard applied here: Newton steps taken with the inverse Hessian to reduce the maximum gradient below 1e-05, which the guidelines describe as stronger evidence of convergence than a maximum gradient or an invertible Hessian alone, while noting that it does not diagnose a local minimum. All `r n_models` models presented here inverted their Hessians (Table \@ref(tab:max-grad)). Every fit that could be polished was polished with Newton steps taken using the inverse Hessian, including the two that already met the conventional threshold of a maximum absolute gradient < 0.001, so that the set is treated consistently. Polishing reduces the gradient without moving the fit: across the models it changed the objective function by no more than 4 x 10^-7^ and moved B~MSY~ and the OFL by no more than 2 parts in 10^7^, the largest movement being in `Model 26.1c`. `Model 25.3`, which was fitted under an earlier version of GMACS and cannot be re-run with the current executable, is reported as originally fitted and retains a maximum gradient of 0.00134. Likelihood components by category for each candidate model are summarized in Tables \@ref(tab:like-index-tot), \@ref(tab:like-comp-tot), and \@ref(tab:like-other-tot).

A zero gradient should not be read as evidence that the parameters are well determined. It states that the fit sits at a stationary point of the likelihood, not that the likelihood is sharply peaked there, and it says nothing about how many other such points exist. The jitter analysis below speaks to the second question, and the near-zero Hessian eigenvalues discussed there to the first.

The practical cost of the multiple optima is visible in `Model 26.1`. The jitter analysis located a solution 1.27 negative log-likelihood units better than the fit obtained from the model's own starting values, a difference that would ordinarily be considered small. Adopting it moved B~MSY~ by less than one percent, but moved the total OFL from 50.27 to 43.83 kt, a change of approximately 13 percent. The choice among solutions that the data separate only weakly therefore carries more consequence for the management quantity than several of the structural choices examined in this assessment.

`r if (!jit_have) "*Jitter results not yet generated; run 05_run_jitter.R to produce them. The paragraphs below will populate from those runs.*"`

As in past cycles, jittering was used to evaluate sensitivity to starting values. `r if (jit_have) sprintf("Of the %s runs, %s produced a complete set of estimates and %s attained a maximum absolute gradient below %s. %s of the runs met the conventional threshold of %s. For comparison, the accepted fit attained %s before Newton polishing and reports a maximum gradient of zero after it (Table \\@ref(tab:max-grad)); the jitter runs above are reported on their unpolished gradients, which is what makes them comparable with one another.", jit_fmt(jit_n,0), jit_fmt(jit_complete,0), jit_fmt(jit_conv,0), format(jit_man$grad_usable), jit_fmt(.js('n_meets_conventional'),0), format(jit_man$grad_conventional), trimws(formatC(.js('base_max_grad'), format='g', digits=3)))`

`r if (jit_have && jit_multimodal) sprintf("The runs settled into %d distinct optima (Figure \\@ref(fig:jitter)), confirming that the multimodality reported in the 2025 preliminary and final assessments persists in the 2026 model. The largest cluster of solutions accounted for %s%% of the runs that reached an optimum, but that cluster is not the best fit: the solution adopted here was reached by only %s of them. Across all runs, the directed OFL ranged from %s to %s kt and mature male biomass in %s ranged from %s to %s kt, so the choice of starting values, not the data, moves the management quantities across that range. The same separation is visible in male recruitment (Figure \\@ref(fig:jitt-rec)) and in MMB (Figure \\@ref(fig:jitt-ssb)).", jit_nmodes, jit_fmt(jit_pct_best,1), jit_fmt(jit_n_at_base,0), jit_fmt(jit_ofl_min,2), jit_fmt(jit_ofl_max,2), jit_fmt(jit_term_yr,0), jit_fmt(jit_mmb_min,1), jit_fmt(jit_mmb_max,1))`
`r if (jit_have && !jit_multimodal) sprintf("The runs settled into a single optimum (Figure \\@ref(fig:jitter)); the multimodality reported in the 2025 preliminary and final assessments is not evident in the 2026 model. The directed OFL across the runs ranged from %s to %s kt and mature male biomass in %s from %s to %s kt, which is the residual spread within one optimum rather than a separation between optima.", jit_fmt(jit_ofl_min,2), jit_fmt(jit_ofl_max,2), jit_fmt(jit_term_yr,0), jit_fmt(jit_mmb_min,1), jit_fmt(jit_mmb_max,1))`

`r if (jit_have && jit_improve > 0.001 && jit_promoted) sprintf("One jitter run found a better fit than the starting solution, improving the negative log likelihood by %s units. Following the convention used in the 2025 assessment, that run was adopted as the reported model and re-fit with the Hessian; all quantities in this document derive from it. The provenance of that fit, including its random seed, is recorded with the model.", jit_fmt(jit_improve,3))`
`r if (jit_have && jit_improve > 0.001 && !jit_promoted) sprintf("One jitter run found a better fit than the reported model, improving the negative log likelihood by %s units. It has not been adopted. [[author: the 2025 assessment reported the lowest-likelihood run of 100 jitters; decide whether to do so here.]]", jit_fmt(jit_improve,3))`
`r if (jit_have && jit_improve <= 0.001) "No jitter run improved materially on the reported fit, which supports the reported solution being the global optimum rather than a local one."`

`r if (jit_have && !is.null(jitter$attribution)) sprintf("The parameters that separate the optima are summarized in Table \\@ref(tab:jitter-attribution) and Figure \\@ref(fig:jitt-attrib). Identifying which parameters differ between the clouds, rather than only observing that the clouds exist, was requested by the SSC and is intended to direct the structural work needed to resolve the multiple optima.")` [[author: interpret the attribution result -- which processes the separating parameters belong to, and what that implies for the structural changes to evaluate before the next cycle.]]

Removing the female population improves the numerical behavior of the model. `Model 26.2` estimates 234 parameters against 412 for `Model 26.1b`. Its accepted fit attains a maximum absolute gradient of zero to reported precision after Newton polishing, and a Hessian markedly better conditioned than that of `Model 26.1b` (condition number 3.3e05 against 1.4e06, smallest eigenvalue 120 against 35), with no non-positive eigenvalues. Jittering the male-only model over 100 runs recovered its accepted fit in `r .f(jit_mo_pct, 1)` percent of the runs that reached an optimum, against `r .f(jit_pct_at_base, 1)` percent for `Model 26.1b`; the multimodality that has characterized this assessment is therefore reduced but not removed by dropping the females. The retrospective pattern is also smaller: Mohn's rho for mature male biomass is -0.09, or -0.08 when the terminal survey year is withheld, against -0.11 for `Model 26.1b`, and both remain inside the Hurtado-Ferro et al. (2015) bounds. The terminal-year recruitment artifact is substantially reduced, with Mohn's rho for male recruitment falling from approximately 8 to 0.7. This is consistent with the expectation that removing the females reduces the confounding among growth, natural mortality, and selectivity. One caveat belongs with it. In `Model 26.2` the base natural mortality offset for immature males is estimated at its lower bound of -1, with a standard error of 2e-05; because M is specified as relative for that group, the bound puts immature-male M at exp(-1) times the mature-male rate, or 0.106 yr^-1^. The same parameter in the accepted two-sex model is estimated at -0.225 with a standard error of 0.117, well inside its range, giving 0.232 yr^-1^. Removing the females is what drives it to the bound, and the bound is binding: the fit is asking for immature males to die at about a third of the mature rate and is being stopped from going lower. That is a structural statement about the model, not a numerical detail. Two consequences follow. Part of the improvement in conditioning is a constraint removing a parameter from estimation rather than a better-determined likelihood, so the gain is smaller than the parameter count alone suggests. And the implied immature-male mortality should not be carried into a specification model without being examined on its own terms. The other parameters at bounds in `Model 26.2` are the three fully-selected trawl-survey size classes, which are at bounds in the two-sex model as well and are not diagnostic. Dropping the females also lowers the reference points: $B_{MSY}$ falls from 144.97 to 131.34 kt and the total-catch OFL from 85.65 to 77.00 kt, with terminal mature male biomass falling from 141.53 to 115.90 kt (Table \@ref(tab:stepchange)).

```{r retro-setup, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Retrospective outputs, written by 06_run_retrospective.R. Every value quoted
# in the narrative below is pulled from these files at knit time so the text
# cannot drift from the runs.
# Follow the accepted model rather than naming a folder. Hardcoded, this would
# report a DIFFERENT model's retrospective without warning if accepted_model
# were repointed -- which it was on 2026-08-28 (see the note above).
retro_dir <- file.path(report_model, "retro")
stopifnot("retro_dir does not exist for the accepted model" = dir.exists(retro_dir))

.rd <- function(f) {
  p <- file.path(retro_dir, f)
  if (file.exists(p)) read.csv(p, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) else NULL
}
retro_rho  <- .rd("mohns_rho.csv")
retro_rel  <- .rd("retro_peel_relative.csv")
retro_diag <- .rd("retro_diagnostics.csv")
# The retrospective reports MMB and recruitment only. There is no
# retro_refpoints.csv: GMACS does not compute reference points for a peeled run
# (gmacsbase.TPL 2.20.34 gates both call sites on nyrRetroNo == 0, :5478 and
# :13625), so every peel returns them as exactly 0. Confirmed 2026-08-27; the
# peels run WITH the Hessian, so this was never a -nohess problem. The terminal
# fit's reference points are in the model directory and retro/base_run.csv.
#
# NOT read here: retro/prj_growth_year_diagnostic.csv. It is a developer
# diagnostic, not an assessment result, and its BMSY = OFL = 0 columns are that
# same peel behavior. Nothing in the SAFE should be able to reach those zeros.

retro_have <- !is.null(retro_rho)

# convenience accessors; return NA (not an error) when the runs are absent
.rho <- function(mode, quantity) {
  if (!retro_have) return(NA_real_)
  v <- retro_rho$mohns_rho[retro_rho$mode == mode & retro_rho$quantity == quantity]
  if (length(v)) v[1] else NA_real_
}
.fmt <- function(x, d = 3) if (is.na(x)) "NA" else formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)

retro_npeel <- if (!is.null(retro_rel)) max(retro_rel$peel) else NA_integer_
retro_yr1   <- if (!is.null(retro_rel)) max(retro_rel$terminal_year) else NA_integer_
retro_yrN   <- if (!is.null(retro_rel)) min(retro_rel$terminal_year) else NA_integer_
```

The guidelines also ask whether any parameters were inestimable or reached their bounds. In the accepted fit no parameter reached a bound and the Hessian is well conditioned: its smallest eigenvalue is 34.6 and none is non-positive. Twenty-four of the 412 estimated parameters have a standard error larger than the absolute value of the estimate. Sixteen of those are estimated within 0.1 of zero, where a large ratio is arithmetic rather than diagnostic: four selectivity offsets, three fishing mortality deviations, two fishing mortality offsets, two recruitment deviations, three recruitment proportion parameters, one growth parameter, and one natural mortality parameter, `M_pars_est[10]`, estimated at 0.022 with a standard error of 0.84. That last one is near zero but is not well determined, and should be read as an identifiability question rather than as arithmetic. The remainder are three recruitment deviations, three recruitment proportion parameters, a fishing mortality deviation, and `M_pars_est[2]`, the natural mortality deviation for mature males in the first event block, estimated at 0.33 with a standard error of 0.59.

That is a property of this fit and not of the model. In cold starts the model can settle in an optimum where the second natural-mortality block for immature females, `M_pars_est[15]`, is unidentified: it drifts toward its upper bound of 10 with a standard error of order 5 x 10^3^, the smallest Hessian eigenvalue falls to 1.1 x 10^-6^ against a next-smallest of 19.8, and the likelihood acquires a single flat direction along which a cold start lands wherever floating-point noise takes it. In the accepted fit that same parameter is estimated at 1.83 with a standard error of 0.58, consistent with its block-one counterpart at 1.80, and the flat direction is absent. Whether an exponential time-varying natural mortality block on immature females is identifiable from these data at all is a question for the Plan Team; the alternative is to fix it, as the corresponding rows for the other sex and maturity combinations already are.

### Retrospective analysis
`r if (!retro_have) "*Retrospective results not yet generated; run 06_run_retrospective.R to produce them.*"`

Retrospective analyses were performed by sequentially removing the terminal year of data from the model, re-fitting, and comparing the resulting time series of estimated mature male biomass with the estimates from the model fit to the full data set. A retrospective pattern is a consistent directional change in an assessment estimate for a given year as additional years of data are added. `r if (retro_have) sprintf("Peels of one through %d years were run, giving terminal years from %d back to %d.", retro_npeel, retro_yr1, retro_yrN)` The peels were not Newton-polished, and none of them meets the maximum-gradient criterion of 0.001 that the accepted fit is held to: across the standard sweep the maximum absolute gradient runs from 0.0015 to 0.020. Mohn's rho below is therefore computed from fits that are at an optimum but not polished to it, which is the normal condition for a retrospective sweep and is stated here so the contrast with the convergence section is not read as an inconsistency.

Mohn's $\rho$ is reported here as the mean across peels of the relative difference between each peel's terminal-year estimate and the estimate for that same year from the model fit to all of the data,

$$\rho = \frac{1}{P}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\frac{X_{T_p,\,p}-X_{T_p,\,0}}{X_{T_p,\,0}},$$

where $T_p$ is the terminal year of peel $p$ and $X_{\cdot,0}$ is the unpeeled fit. A positive $\rho$ therefore means the peels sit *above* the full model, i.e. that terminal biomass is revised downward as data accumulate. Hurtado-Ferro et al. (2015) suggest that $\rho$ outside $[-0.22,\,0.30]$ for a short-lived stock indicates a retrospective pattern worth reporting.

Two retrospectives are presented. The **standard** retrospective removes the last $p$ years of all data streams. The **dropped-terminal-survey** retrospective additionally withholds the most recent survey year, which isolates the leverage of the single most recent survey observation on the terminal estimate. This distinction matters for this stock because, under the crab-year convention, an assessment with end year $N$ is fit to the summer survey from year $N+1$, so the terminal MMB estimate rests heavily on one very recent survey point.

`r if (retro_have) sprintf("For mature male biomass, the standard retrospective gave Mohn's $\\rho$ = %s and the dropped-terminal-survey retrospective gave $\\rho$ = %s (Table \\@ref(tab:retro-rho), Figures \\@ref(fig:retro-mmb) and \\@ref(fig:retro-drop-survey)). Male recruitment gave $\\rho$ = %s.", .fmt(.rho("standard","mature_male_biomass")), .fmt(.rho("drop_survey","mature_male_biomass")), .fmt(.rho("standard","recruitment_male")))`

Management quantities are not recomputed for each peel. GMACS calculates reference points only when the retrospective peel count is zero (`gmacsbase.TPL` 2.20.34 gates both call sites on `nyrRetroNo == 0`), so every peeled run returns $B_{MSY}$, $B/B_{MSY}$ and the OFL as exactly zero rather than as estimates. This is a property of GMACS and not of the runs presented here -- the peels were fit with the Hessian -- and it applies equally to the 2025 assessment. The retrospective therefore characterizes mature male biomass and recruitment only, and the movement in the management advice itself under each peel cannot be read from it. [[author: if the CPT wants the advice-level retrospective for a scientific-uncertainty buffer, it needs peel-by-peel reference points computed outside GMACS.]]

<!-- >>> REVIEW: once the peels are final, characterize the DIRECTION and PRACTICAL
     SIGNIFICANCE of the pattern here in words (the numbers above are pulled
     automatically, but the interpretation is an author judgement). Also state
     whether the retrospective motivates any change to the ABC buffer. -->

Each peel was re-fit with the Hessian, and each was started from the accepted fit's parameter vector rather than from a cold start. Seeding matters in a likelihood with this many optima: cold-started, a peel measures which optimum it happened to fall into as much as it measures the retrospective pattern. It does, however, compress the pattern relative to an unseeded sweep, and the values below should be read with that in mind. The projection file was left unmodified; GMACS shifts its reference-point averaging windows back by the number of peeled years internally.

### Historical analysis

The retrospective analysis above withholds data from a single model. A historical analysis asks a different question: how the perception of the stock has changed across successive assessments accepted for management. Figure \@ref(fig:historical-mmb) shows estimated mature male biomass at mating as each assessment from 2016 to 2025 saw it.

The revisions are large, and they are much larger than the within-model retrospective pattern. The clearest case is the collapse itself. The 2020 assessment put mature male biomass at the time of the survey in 2020 at 486.5 kt; the 2021 assessment, with the 2021 survey in hand, revised that same year to 40.95 kt, a downward revision of 92 percent. The revision then reversed: the 2022 assessment estimated 2020 biomass at mating at 19.1 kt, and the 2023 assessment revised the same year to 205.4 kt, an order-of-magnitude increase in the opposite direction. Terminal-year estimates across the ten vintages range from 26.7 kt (2021 assessment) to 207.2 kt (2020 assessment).

[[author: the guidelines ask for the cause of any obvious differences, and that cause cannot be established from the material in this repository -- `data/historical/` holds the published time series but not the configurations that produced them. The candidates worth checking against the 2021--2023 assessment documents are the treatment of the 2018--19 mortality event, changes in the maturity input, and any change in the initialization. Note that the time-varying probability of terminal molt is not itself new this cycle; what changed for 2026 is the workflow producing it.]]

The practical consequence for management advice is that terminal-year mature male biomass in this assessment has historically been revised by considerably more than the within-model retrospective analysis implies, and in both directions. [[author: the guidelines ask for uncertainty intervals on the vintages. The published series in `data/historical/` carry point estimates only, so the figure shows no intervals; either recover the intervals from the archived assessments or state here that they were not available.]]

knitr::include_graphics("plots/historical_mating_mmb_est.png")
```

### Model fits
Fits to the survey indices of mature biomass were broadly similar across the models (Figure \@ref(fig:mmbfits)). `Model 26.1b`, the only two-sex model carrying the 2026 survey, continues to have difficulty fitting the terminal year of female biomass; `Model 26.2` estimates no female population, so the question does not arise for it. Inputting a yearly varying probability of terminal molt from the new maturity workflow, which every model other than `Model 25.3` carries, shifts the estimated population dynamics modestly but does not resolve the female terminal-year fit (Figure \@ref(fig:mmbfits)).

[[author: this paragraph described the hybrid-survey and `imm_surv` candidates, which are not in the September set -- the CPT and SSC advised against both in May and June 2026. Replace with a comparison across the six models actually presented, or drop it.]]

Fits to the non-directed fishery catches were good for all models (Figure \@ref(fig:catchfits)). Fits to the directed-fishery retained catch were also good across the model set. [[author: a sentence here compared discard fits in the hybrid-fishery models, which are not in the September set. Removed rather than left describing models the document does not present. The underlying observation -- that ADF&G reported roughly 18 kt of legal-male hybrid catch in 1997, with hybrid identification quality decreasing further back in the time series -- is still recorded in Table \@ref(tab:obscatch) and may be worth keeping somewhere.]] The models accommodate the additional discards primarily through changes in estimated discard fishing mortality rather than through major changes in selectivity.

Differences among models in the fits to size composition data for retained catch in the directed fishery are small (size composition figures, below). No visually discernible differences among models existed for female discards from the directed fishery. Fits to the non-directed fishery had some of the largest misfits of all data sources (particularly for male data), but this is unsurprising given a single estimated selectivity curve and changes in fishery behavior over time. Sample sizes are assumed to be 100 for all composition data except for female discards in 2021, 2024 and 2025 (sample size = 10).

Fits to the survey size composition data were broadly similar across models in most years (size composition figures, below). The plus-group change (extending the plus group to all crab > 135 mm) makes a small visual difference for retained males but improves the runtime of the model substantially. All models had difficulty fitting the size composition data for immature females in 2009 and 2019, which could suggest some unmodeled size-based mortality or time-varying probability of terminal molt. Estimates of mean growth are shown in Figure \@ref(fig:growthfits).

### Estimated population processes
The estimated abundance of commercially preferred male crab (> 101 mm carapace width) varied among models (Figure \@ref(fig:obs-101-vs-pred)). The early years during which differences in survey selectivity occurred were particularly different. All models agreed that the abundance in recent years has been the lowest in the time series (Figure \@ref(fig:obs-101-vs-pred-bio)). The estimates of the most recent era of survey selectivity were similar across models for both sexes (Figure \@ref(fig:select-prior)).

Estimated fisheries selectivities were similar across models (Figure \@ref(fig:predselectfish)). Estimated fully-selected fishing mortality for the directed fishery was highly variable and relatively high for most of the fishery history (Figure \@ref(fig:predfmort)). The total fishery selectivity curve is shifted far to the right, so only the largest crab experience the fully-selected fishing mortality. 

The probability of undergoing terminal molt is input as data (Figure \@ref(fig:predmat)); the status quo workflow produces a strong increasing trend through time at intermediate sizes (e.g., at 77 mm the probability rose from ~0.2 in the early 1990s to ~0.5 after 2010), while [[VERIFY: this comparison of the two maturity workflows -- the quoted probabilities at 77 mm and the characterization of one trend as strong and the other as weak -- could not be reproduced from the terminal-molt arrays in the control files. Check it against the workflow output directly before this goes out.]] the new maturity workflow produces a much weaker temporal trend (~0.35--0.45 throughout the time series). The new workflow uses a spatiotemporal `sdmTMB` model fit to chela-based maturity classifications and borrows information across years and locations for size bins with sparse chela data; it does not extrapolate the predicted spatial probability surface beyond stations with measured crab.

Trends in recruitment were very similar across models for the early time series, with some variability in scale and differences in timing between the sexes (Figure \@ref(fig:recruits)). Differences in estimated recruitment in the most recent years were observed among models for males and contribute to differences in OFLs across the model set.

Base estimates of natural mortality for mature animals of both sexes were broadly similar across the models presented (Figure \@ref(fig:nat-m), Table \@ref(tab:stepchange)). All models estimated additional mortality events that removed a large fraction of crab by sex and maturity state, except for mature females, at some point during the marine heatwave of 2018--19. In the inferior optima reached from cold starts the immature-female natural mortality deviation for the second event block is poorly determined, with a standard error far larger than the estimate itself; in the accepted fit it is not, as reported under model convergence, where whether it should be fixed rather than estimated is also discussed. [[author: the May document also reported an extreme immature-female M in one of the hybrid candidates; those models are not carried forward, so that observation has been removed rather than restated.]]

### MMB and management quantities
Estimated mature male biomass time series had similar trends across models but differed in scale (Figure \@ref(fig:predmmb)). Estimates of $B_{MSY}$, current MMB relative to $B_{MSY}$, $F_{MSY}$, $F_{OFL}$ and the Tier 3 OFL are summarized in Table \@ref(tab:stepchange). Across the models presented, the $B_{MSY}$ proxy ranged from 131.3 to 180.1 kt and terminal mature male biomass from 86.9 to 141.5 kt. The three models whose data end in 2024 place the stock below its $B_{MSY}$ proxy (status 0.81 to 0.96), while the two carrying the 2025 fishery and 2026 survey place it above (status 1.23 and 1.32); the additional year of data, rather than any structural change, accounts for that difference. `Model 26.1c`, whose data end in 2019, sits just above the proxy at 1.05, but its reference points are computed from a different span of data and are not comparable with the others.

# F. Calculation of the OFL
## Methodology for OFL 
### Tier 3
Historically, the Tier 3 OFL was calculated using proxies for biomass and fishing mortality reference points and a sloped control rule. Proxies for biomass and fishing mortality reference points were calculated using spawning-biomass-per-recruit methods (e.g. Clark, 1991). After fitting the assessment model to the data and estimating population parameters, the model was projected forward 100 years using the estimated parameters under no exploitation and constant recruitment to determine 'unfished' mature male biomass-per-recruit. Projections were repeated in which the bisection method was used to identify a fishing mortality that reduced the mature male biomass-per-recruit to 35% of the unfished level (i.e. F~35%~ and B~35%~). Calculations of F~*35%*~ were made under the assumption that bycatch fishing mortality was equal to the estimated average value over the last 10 years. 

Calculated values of F~35%~ and B~35%~ were used in conjunction with a Tier 3 control rule to adjust the proportion of F~35%~ that is applied to the stock based on the status of the population relative to B~35%~ (Amendment 24, NMFS). To determine the F~OFL~, the population is projected to the time of fishing for the upcoming fishery under no fishing. If the MMB at that time exceeds 25% of B~35%~, a fishery can occur and the F~OFL~ is calculated as:

$$\begin{equation}
F_{OFL} =
\begin{cases}
Bycatch  & if \frac{MMB}{B_{35}} \leq 0.25 \\[3ex]
\frac {F_{35} ( \frac {MMB}{B_{35}} - \alpha)}{1-\alpha}  & if 0.25 < \frac {MMB}{B_{35}} < 1 \\[3ex]
F_{35} & if MMB > B_{35}
\end{cases}
\end{equation}$$

Where MMB is the projected morphometrically mature male biomass in the current survey year after fishing at the F~*OFL*~, B~*35%*~ is the mature male biomass at the time of mating resulting from fishing at F~*35%*~, F~*35%*~ is the fishing mortality that reduces the morphometrically mature male biomass per recruit to 35% of unfished levels, and $\alpha$ determines the slope of the descending limb of the harvest control rule (set to 0.1 here).

Calculated total Tier 3 OFLs across the models presented ranged from 43.8 to 147.3 kt (Table \@ref(tab:stepchange)). For reference, the observed survey biomass of morphometrically mature males in 2025 was `r .f(survey_morph_2025, 1)` kt and of preferred males (> 101 mm) `r .f(survey_pref_2025, 1)` kt. Taking `Model 26.1`, the model accepted in May, as the comparison baseline at 43.8 kt: correcting the size-composition bin convention and the growth transcription error (`Model 26.1a`) lowered the $B_{MSY}$ proxy from 172.7 to 158.7 kt and raised the OFL to 53.7 kt; adding the 2025 fishery and 2026 survey (`Model 26.1b`) lowered the proxy further to 145.0 kt, raised status above one, and raised the OFL to 85.6 kt. The male-only sensitivity gives a lower OFL than the model it is derived from, 77.0 kt against 85.6 kt. The run truncated to 2019 is not comparable with the others, since its reference points are computed from a different span of data. [[author: interpret the direction of these changes -- in particular why the corrected bin convention and the additional year of data both lower the $B_{MSY}$ proxy.]]

### Tier 4

The Tier 4 calculation is the basis for the 2026 harvest specification. The SSC assigned this stock to **Tier 4b** when it set the 2025/26 specification (October 2025 SSC report, Table 2), and that subtier is carried here. [[author: confirm 4b still applies on this cycle's status.]] A random-effects model (REMA) is fitted to the observed survey biomass series, the B~MSY~ proxy is taken as the mean of the smoothed series, and stock status is the terminal smoothed biomass relative to that proxy. Target fishing mortality is F = M = `r .f(NAT_M, 2)` yr^-1^, the median of the prior on natural mortality.

The averaging period for the B~MSY~ proxy is the whole survey time series, `r .fy(BMSY_WINDOW_LAB)`. The proxy is intended to represent the long-term average productivity of the stock, and there is no basis for withholding the most recent observation from that average; the September 2025 assessment averaged 1982 to 2024, that is, every year but the terminal one. The average is taken over the smoothed series rather than the observations, which is what supplies a value for 2020, when the survey was cancelled. Recomputing this cycle's smoothed series on the narrower 1982--2024 window, for comparison, gives a B~MSY~ proxy of 148.18 kt and a status of 0.769 against the `r .f(bmsy_2026, 2)` kt and `r .f(status_2026, 3)` reported here. Those two comparison figures are this assessment's own REMA fit evaluated on the earlier window; they are not values the September 2025 assessment published, which reported the window and the resulting OFLs but no proxy or status. It does not change the recommended OFL, which applies a flat F = M to the terminal biomass and does not depend on the proxy. It moves only the quantities that do depend on it: the minimum stock size threshold falls from 74.09 to `r .f(msst_2026, 2)` kt, and the ramped alternative rises from 22.87 to `r .f(ofl_2026_ramp_linear, 2)` kt on the linear catch equation both figures were computed with. (The ramped OFL reported in Table \@ref(tab:tier4-currencies), `r .f(ofl_2026_ramp, 2)` kt, is lower again because it also carries the change to the Baranov equation described below.)

Three currencies are carried, as in the September 2025 assessment: morphometrically mature males, large males (>= 95 mm carapace width), and preferred males (> 101 mm). The observed survey biomass for each, in the terminal survey year and the year preceding it, is:
