The recommended currency is morphometrically mature male biomass, giving an OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026)` kt and, after the `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*(1-ABC_buffer))` buffer, an ABC of `r .f(abc_2026)` kt. [[author: the September 2025 assessment recommended the >= 95 mm currency instead, on the grounds that morphometrically mature male biomass "results in reference points that allow for the complete removal of large males". The choice of currency moves the OFL by a factor of `r .f(ofl_curr_ratio, 0)` (Table \@ref(tab:tier4-currencies)) -- far more than either the control-rule or catch-equation choice, and enough that on either large-male currency the OFL would be below `r .f(max(tier4_by_currency$OFL[tier4_by_currency$currency != "morphometric"]), 1)` kt -- so the reversal needs an explicit justification here.]]

The biomass the control rule acts on carries real uncertainty, and the guidelines require it to be reported. The random-effects fit puts terminal morphometrically mature male biomass at `r .f(mmb_2026, 2)` kt with a 95 percent interval of `r .f(mmb_2026_lci, 2)` to `r .f(mmb_2026_uci, 2)` kt, a coefficient of variation of `r .f(100*mmb_2026_cv, 1)` percent. This is the prediction interval REMA returns for the smoothed series, which reflects the process error the random-effects model estimates. It is not the sampling uncertainty of the survey itself: the survey CVs are an input to the fit, not its output, and the two should not be quoted interchangeably. The interval is lognormal, so the log-scale standard deviation is recovered as (log of the upper bound minus log of the lower bound) divided by 2 x 1.96, and the coefficient of variation follows from it.

Propagating that interval through the control rule and the catch equation gives an OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt with a range of `r .f(ofl_2026_lci, 2)` to `r .f(ofl_2026_uci, 2)` kt. That range is wider than the biomass interval alone would imply, because under the sloped rule F~OFL~ rises with status as well: at the lower bound the rate falls to `r .f(t4_rec$Fofl_lci, 3)` and at the upper bound it reaches M itself, `r .f(t4_rec$Fofl_uci, 3)`, so biomass and rate move together in both directions. The OFL is consequently more sensitive to the biomass estimate under this rule than under a flat rate. The corresponding stock status is `r .f(status_2026, 3)` with a range of `r .f(status_2026_lci, 3)` to `r .f(status_2026_uci, 3)`. Two features of that status range matter. The lower bound remains above the minimum stock size threshold of `r .f(msst_2026, 2)` kt, so the stock is not overfished at any point in the interval. But the upper bound reaches `r .f(status_2026_uci, 3)`, so on this measure the biomass at which the stock would be considered rebuilt lies inside the interval, even though the point estimate sits below it. The rebuilding determination in Section H should be read with that in mind.

[[author: this interval covers the random-effects smoothing only. It does not include uncertainty in the B~MSY~ proxy, which is the mean of the same smoothed series and is therefore correlated with the terminal estimate, nor uncertainty in the choice of currency or averaging window, both of which move the OFL by more than this interval does. Say so, or widen the treatment.]]

The recommended basis makes two choices, and each is reported here with its alternative so that the effect of either can be read directly.

**The control rule is the sloped Tier 4 rule from the crab FMP**, under which F~OFL~ ramps linearly from zero at the closure threshold to M at the B~MSY~ proxy: F~OFL~ = M (B/B~MSY~ - alpha) / (1 - alpha), with alpha = 0.10 and a closure threshold beta = 0.25. At the current status of `r .f(status_2026, 3)` this gives F~OFL~ = `r .f(fofl_2026, 4)` against M = `r .f(NAT_M, 2)`.

This is the FMP form, and adopting it resolves a divergence that has stood since last cycle. The September 2025 assessment applied a flat rate and stated that no kink exists in its harvest control rule. The October 2025 SSC identified that as an incomplete implementation --- "full implementation of a Tier 4 crab assessment as specified in the FMP requires application of a harvest control rule" --- and asked the author to recompute the OFL under the control rule during the meeting. The result of that recomputation, F~OFL~ = 0.19 and an OFL of 20.11 kt, is the specification the SSC adopted for 2025/26. The rule applied here is the same one, so this assessment and the specification the Council acted on now rest on the same control rule.

The flat alternative, F~OFL~ = M above the closure threshold with no ramp, is reported alongside: it raises F~OFL~ to `r .f(fofl_2026_flat, 4)` and the OFL from `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` to `r .f(ofl_2026_flat, 2)` kt, a difference of `r .f(100*(ofl_2026_flat/ofl_2026 - 1), 0)` percent. It is not recommended. It should also be noted that the flat form has sometimes been defended by analogy with the groundfish Tier 5 rule, under which the target rate is the natural mortality rate itself with no ramp. That analogy is not available to this stock in any case: the crab and groundfish FMPs define separate and independent tier systems, and a crab stock assessed under crab Tier 4 takes the crab Tier 4 control rule.

**The catch equation is Baranov**, changed this cycle from the linear form used previously. F~OFL~ is an instantaneous rate --- it is set equal to M, which is itself instantaneous --- and natural mortality acts on the stock over the same year, so the yield taken by fishing is F's share of the total mortality Z = F + M rather than the whole of F applied to the biomass at the start of it. The linear form F~OFL~ x B is the first-order approximation to that and always overstates the catch; the overstatement is at its largest precisely here, because setting F~OFL~ = M makes fishing exactly half of Z. On this cycle's biomass, holding the rate at F~OFL~ = M so that only the equation changes, the linear form gives `r .f(ofl_2026_linear, 2)` kt against `r .f(ofl_2026_flat, 2)` kt on Baranov, a difference of `r .f(100*(ofl_2026_linear/ofl_2026_flat - 1), 0)` percent that is the effect of the catch equation alone. The linear form is retained in Table \@ref(tab:tier4-currencies) because the other BSAI crab Tier 4 assessments use it and the comparison across stocks is worth keeping visible.

Both choices differ from the basis the SSC used when it set the 2025/26 specification, and the difference runs in opposite directions, so it is worth setting out. At a stock status of 0.74 the SSC reported F~OFL~ = 0.19 (October 2025 SSC report, Table 2), where flat F = M would have given 0.27: the sloped rule at that status returns M x (0.74 - 0.10) / (1 - 0.10) = 0.192, and the specified OFL of 20.11 kt divided by the MMB of 105.213 kt implies 0.1911, so that specification was set on the **sloped** rule and the **linear** equation. This assessment applies that same sloped rule, so the control rule is no longer a point of divergence; the remaining difference is the catch equation, which lowers the OFL relative to the linear form the SSC used. [[author: the change of catch equation will still be asked about. The mortality argument for Baranov is recorded above; state in your own terms why it is the right basis for a stock that is below B~MSY~ and in a rebuilding plan.]]


## Parameters estimated independently of the assessment

The Tier 4 calculation does not estimate biological parameters. The quantities it takes as given, and their sources, are:

* **Natural mortality**, M = `r .f(NAT_M, 2)` yr^-1^ for mature males. This is the median of the prior on natural mortality used in the integrated assessment, and it is the target fishing mortality at the B~MSY~ proxy and the ceiling from which the Tier 4 control rule ramps down below it.
* **The probability of terminal molt at size**, supplied as a fixed input from the Kodiak laboratory's spatiotemporal `sdmTMB` maturity workflow rather than estimated within the model.
* **The variance in the growth increment**, specified rather than estimated. Mean growth per molt is estimated *within* the assessment, and the model is fit to the growth data (Figure \@ref(fig:growthfits)); it is only the variability about the predicted post-molt size that is fixed.
* **Weight at length**, specified from the published relationship.
* **Discard and bycatch mortality rates**, specified rather than estimated.

## Status determination

**Is the stock subject to overfishing?** No. Overfishing is determined by comparing the catch from the most recent complete crab year with the OFL specified for that year. Total catch in 2025/26 was 7.10 kt --- 4.13 kt retained, 2.52 kt of male and 0.03 kt of female discarded catch from the directed fishery, and 0.42 kt of non-directed bycatch, of which 0.04 kt was taken in the groundfish trawl fisheries and 0.38 kt in other crab fisheries. These are catches, not mortalities: the 30 percent handling mortality on directed discards is applied inside the assessment model rather than to its inputs. Total catch is compared against the OFL of 20.11 kt that the SSC specified for 2025/26 in October 2025. Catch was 35 percent of the specified OFL.

**Is the stock overfished?** The stock was determined to be overfished for 2024/25, with mature male biomass of 60.08 kt against a minimum stock size threshold of 71.40 kt (October 2025 SSC report, Table 1), and it remains in the rebuilding plan adopted under Amendment 53. On this cycle's estimate mature male biomass is `r .f(mmb_2026, 2)` kt against a minimum stock size threshold of `r .f(msst_2026, 2)` kt, so the stock is above the threshold on the current estimate and across the whole of its 95 percent interval (Section F).

**Is the stock approaching an overfished condition?** Unknown.

[[author: the two totals differ by exactly the non-directed bycatch. The SSC's Table 1 gives 2.81 kt for 2024/25; retained 2.145 + directed male discards 0.663 + female discards 0.00002 = 2.809, so the SSC's figure is directed-fishery catch only, while the 7.10 kt reported here for 2025/26 includes 0.42 kt of non-directed bycatch. The determination is unaffected --- catch is far below the OFL either way --- but Table 1 currently mixes the two conventions between its 2024/25 and 2025/26 rows. Settle which one the column carries.]]

\newpage

## F~limit~

Under the Tier 4 control rule the fishing mortality rate above which the stock is considered to be subject to overfishing is the natural mortality rate itself when biomass is at or above the B~MSY~ proxy; under the FMP form it is reduced along the ramp below that point. This document applies the FMP ramp (Section F), so at the current status of `r .f(status_2026, 3)` the stock's F~limit~ is `r .f(fofl_2026, 3)` yr^-1^ rather than M itself. Under the flat alternative it would be M = `r .f(NAT_M, 2)` yr^-1^ across the whole range above the closure threshold. This is a different quantity from the reverse-engineered F reported for Tier 1--3 stocks, which is the rate that would have produced a catch equal to the previous year's OFL, and that quantity is not computed here.

\newpage

# G. Calculation of the ABC

The recommended acceptable biological catch (ABC) is calculated by subtracting a buffer from the OFL to account for scientific uncertainty. The buffer applied here is `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*(1-ABC_buffer))` percent, giving an ABC of `r .f(abc_2026, 2)` kt against an OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt.

[[author: the justification for the buffer goes here. Note that the sentence previously in this place --- that the buffer covers "retrospective patterns and model misspecification" --- is a Tier 3 rationale and does not apply: the recommended OFL is not output of an assessment model at all. The uncertainties this buffer is actually carrying are the ones set out in Section F: the random-effects process error on the smoothed biomass (a CV of `r .f(100*mmb_2026_cv, 1)` percent, giving a 95 percent interval of `r .f(mmb_2026_lci, 1)` to `r .f(mmb_2026_uci, 1)` kt), the choice of currency, which moves the OFL by a factor of `r .f(ofl_curr_ratio, 0)`, the choice of control rule, and the unattributed hybrid component of retained catch discussed in Section B.]]

The maximum permissible ABC is reported regardless of the author's recommendation (groundfish guidelines 4.11.2; the crab checklist requires the same). Under the ABC control rule it is the P\*-quantile of the OFL probability distribution presented in the Executive Summary, where P\* is the acceptable probability that the ABC-level catch exceeds the true OFL. At the June 2026 SSC's default of P\* = `r .f(PSTAR_CRAB, 2)` for crab stocks this gives a maximum permissible ABC of `r .f(maxabc_2026, 2)` kt, `r .f(100*(1 - maxabc_2026/ofl_2026), 1)` percent below the OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt. That buffer is minimal, as the June 2026 SSC noted the default crab control rule returns, because a P\* just below one-half places the quantile just below the median of the distribution. The recommended ABC of `r .f(abc_2026, 2)` kt, carrying the `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*(1-ABC_buffer))` percent buffer justified below, is `r .f(100*(1 - abc_2026/maxabc_2026), 1)` percent below the maximum permissible value, so the recommendation is the more precautionary of the two. [[author: confirm P\* = 0.49 is the value to apply for this stock, and that the P\*-quantile of the OFL distribution is the intended maxABC construction rather than a fixed maximum buffer on the OFL.]]

The June 2026 SSC supported reporting a stock-specific history of the buffers applied to the OFL, and supported the CPT's suggestion that a historical buffer could initially be set at the average buffer from the previous five assessments (Table \@ref(tab:buffer-history)).

```{r buffer-history, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}
# Five years, 2021-2025: the checklist asks for a five-year buffer history and
# the June 2026 SSC proposes "the average buffer from the previous five
# assessments". 2021 as printed in the 2025 SAFE; 2022-2025 from Table 2 of each
# October SSC report -- the 2022 report was thought unavailable and its 25% was
# NA until it was located (2026-08-29).
buffer_hist <- data.frame(
  Year   = c(2021L, 2022L, 2023L, 2024L, 2025L),
  Buffer = c(25, 25, 50, 65, 40),
  Source = c("2025 SAFE, Section G",
             "October 2022 SSC report, Table 2",
             "October 2023 SSC report, Table 2",
             "October 2024 SSC report, Table 2",
             "October 2025 SSC report, Table 2"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
.known <- buffer_hist$Buffer[!is.na(buffer_hist$Buffer)]
buffer_hist$Buffer <- ifelse(is.na(buffer_hist$Buffer), "NA",
                             sprintf("%.0f%%", buffer_hist$Buffer))
names(buffer_hist)[2] <- "SSC buffer (% of OFL)"

flextable::flextable(buffer_hist) |>
  # Crab years, not measurements: flextable's default integer formatting applies
  # big.mark and printed them "2,020" (fixed 2026-08-29).
  flextable::colformat_int(j = "Year", big.mark = "") |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = sprintf(paste("History of the ABC buffer applied by the SSC, as a percentage of the",
                            "OFL, for the %d most recent assessments. The mean is %.0f%%.",
                            "Each value is read from Table 2 of the October SSC report for that",
                            "year, except 2021, which is as printed in the September",
                            "2025 assessment."),
                      length(.known), mean(.known)),
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "buffer-history")
  )
```

The `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*(1-ABC_buffer))` percent buffer recommended here is the figure the September 2025 assessment also recommended, and is the buffer historically applied to crab stocks whose data and model complexity are sufficient for Tier 3. It is lower than the buffer the SSC has applied to this stock in recent years. For the 2025/26 specification the SSC applied a 40 percent buffer, setting an ABC of 12.07 kt against an OFL of 20.11 kt (October 2025 SSC report, Table 2), and against the history in Table \@ref(tab:buffer-history) a 20 percent buffer would be the smallest applied to this stock in any of the five years shown, and a little over half the `r sprintf("%.0f", mean(.known))` percent average across them. The consequence is worth stating plainly, because it is the first comparison the record invites. The recommended OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt is `r if (mp_have) sprintf("%.0f", abs(100*(ofl_2026/mp$ofl[mp$crab_year == "2025/26"] - 1))) else "NA"` percent **below** the `r if (mp_have) .f(mp$ofl[mp$crab_year == "2025/26"], 2) else "NA"` kt specified for 2025/26, yet the recommended ABC of `r .f(abc_2026, 2)` kt is `r if (mp_have) sprintf("%.0f", 100*(abc_2026/mp$abc[mp$crab_year == "2025/26"] - 1)) else "NA"` percent **above** the `r if (mp_have) .f(mp$abc[mp$crab_year == "2025/26"], 2) else "NA"` kt specified. The OFL and the ABC move in opposite directions because the buffer halves, from 40 percent to 20; the buffer is doing all of that work. Meanwhile the biomass the control rule acts on is close to unchanged --- the smoothed mature-male series rises about 4 percent and the survey observation behind it falls about 3 percent (Figure \@ref(fig:rema-fit)). The rise in the ABC is therefore entirely a consequence of the buffer rather than of a change in the stock or in the control rule, and should be presented as such. The contrast is sharper still against the industry currency: preferred-male biomass fell `r .f(abs(pref_biom_chg), 1)` percent over the same year, to the `r if (!is.na(pref_rank_2026)) paste0(pref_rank_2026, if (pref_rank_2026 %% 10 == 1 && pref_rank_2026 != 11) 'st' else if (pref_rank_2026 %% 10 == 2 && pref_rank_2026 != 12) 'nd' else if (pref_rank_2026 %% 10 == 3 && pref_rank_2026 != 13) 'rd' else 'th') else 'NA'` lowest value in `r pref_n_yrs` years (Table \@ref(tab:survey-currencies)). A recommendation that raises the ABC by `r if (mp_have) sprintf("%.0f", 100*(abc_2026/mp$abc[mp$crab_year == "2025/26"] - 1)) else "NA"` percent in a year when the marketable component of the stock fell by that much will be questioned, and with the control rule no longer in dispute the answer rests on the buffer and on the currency argument in Section F rather than on any claim about stock trend. Three of the four risk table categories score Level 1, Normal (Table \@ref(tab:risk-table)). [[author: with the sloped rule adopted, the buffer is now the single largest departure in this document from the last specification, and it is no longer offset by anything: the change to the Baranov catch equation moves the ABC the same way the OFL moves, down. The recommended ABC is `r .f(abc_2026, 2)` kt where the basis the SSC used for 2025/26 -- same sloped rule, linear equation, 40 percent buffer -- would give `r .f(0.6*ofl_2026_ramp_linear, 2)` kt on this cycle's biomass, a factor of `r .f(abc_2026/(0.6*ofl_2026_ramp_linear), 2)`. Essentially all of that gap is the buffer. That is the number the CPT will arrive at, so the document should reach it first. It needs your argument, and the assessment-related risk category -- still unscored -- is where the supporting evidence for it belongs. The June 2026 SSC cautioned against a predetermined direction in modifying any buffer.]]

## Risk table

The risk table follows the four categories used for groundfish, in the tiered form the June 2026 SSC described: a long-term row capturing persistent uncertainty, which is what justifies a base or historical buffer, and a current-year row for year-specific risk. The SSC scopes the long-term row to the assessment and population-dynamics categories only, which is why the ecosystem and fishery cells in that row are not scored.

The population-dynamics, ecosystem and fishery-informed cells below are taken from the 2026 risk table summary prepared from the ESP (Fedewa and Shotwell 2026), the AFSC Spring Preview of Ecosystem and Economic Conditions Workshop, and the eastern Bering Sea Ecosystem Status Report (Siddon 2026, in press). The ESP is Appendix A to this assessment.

```{r risk-table, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}
# Grid transcribed from 'Snow Crab ESP-ESR Risk Table Summary 2026.docx'. The
# three assessment-related cells were left for the author there; the evidence
# is supplied here and the LEVEL is not, because the level drives the buffer.
risk_tab <- data.frame(
  Category = c("Assessment-related", "Population dynamics",
               "Ecosystem", "Fishery-informed stock"),
  `Long-term / persistent` = c(
    paste("[[author: assign a level. The evidence: multimodality has persisted across cycles and is",
          "the reason the stock moved from Tier 3 to Tier 4. Jittering the accepted model returns to",
          "the reported fit in only 1.3 percent of converged runs, and to the best lettered mode --- a",
          "different and inferior optimum --- in 5.1 percent. A likelihood improvement of 1.27 units moved the OFL",
          "of Model 26.1 by 12.8 percent. Successive assessments have revised the same historical",
          "years by up to an order of magnitude (Section E, Historical analysis), which is far larger",
          "than the within-model retrospective pattern. The base model estimates on the order of four",
          "hundred parameters, many highly correlated, which the June 2026 SSC identified as",
          "consistent with overparameterization.]]"),
    "[[author: assign a level and supporting evidence. Not scored in the ESP summary.]]",
    "Not scored (long-term row is scoped to the first two categories)",
    "Not scored (long-term row is scoped to the first two categories)"),
  `Current year` = c(
    paste("[[author: assign a level. The evidence: the OFL rests on a Tier 4 calculation whose terminal",
          "biomass carries a CV of 14.8 percent, a 95 percent interval of 85.4 to 152.1 kt, and a",
          "status interval of 0.58 to 1.04 that spans the rebuilt threshold. Three specification choices",
          sprintf("move the OFL by more than that interval does: the currency, by a factor of %.0f,",
                  ofl_curr_ratio),
          "the control rule, which lowers it from 23.8 to 18.4 kt, and the catch equation, on which the",
          "linear form used through 2025 would give 30.8 kt. Against that, every model that could be polished",
          "attains a zero maximum gradient and all Hessians inverted, and Mohn's rho for mature male",
          "biomass stays inside the Hurtado-Ferro bounds -- though the rho for recruitment does not,",
          "at 7.9 standard and 9.5 with the terminal survey withheld.]]"),
    paste("Level 1: Normal. Stock-specific indicators related to natural mortality, growth and",
          "recruitment suggest no apparent population dynamics concerns, although a highly",
          "female-skewed sex ratio combined with directional downward shifts in male maturity and",
          "depressed abundances of large males should continue to be monitored."),
    paste("Level 1: Normal. Thermal conditions from winter 2025 to summer 2026 have been favorable,",
          "with an extensive cold pool and high sea ice extent. Pelagic feeding conditions have",
          "remained favorable since 2023; benthic prey indicators were mixed in 2025. Competition for",
          "space remained high, competition for prey low. Predation pressure from Pacific cod was",
          "reduced in 2025. Spring 2026 offshelf transport moved crab away from suitable benthic",
          "habitat. Overall, ecosystem concerns are minor with uncertain impacts on the stock."),
    paste("Level 1: Normal. Fishery-informed indicators generally support stable stock condition.",
          "Shifts in fleet behavior appear motivated primarily by weather, sorting, fuel costs and",
          "TAC considerations rather than stock health or distribution. Many skippers noted increased",
          "hybrid abundance during the 2025/26 fishery, consistent with the dramatic increase in",

flextable::flextable(risk_tab) |>
  # Four multi-line rows, so this table breaks across a page. Suppress the

## Author recommendations

The June 2026 SSC recommended that only the Tier 4 model be brought forward in October, to allow time for the development of a simpler and more stable Tier 3 model. The overfishing limit in this document is calculated on that basis. The Tier 3 models are presented to document progress and are not proposed for specification.

Three questions the May 2026 preliminary assessment put to the CPT and SSC have since been settled and are not reopened here. The composition correction and the expanded plus group were endorsed as technical corrections and are carried in every September model. The immature survey index was rejected as a convergence fix, on the grounds that it shifts the model toward higher natural mortality among mature males and raises a question of duplicative use of the same survey data. Hybrid catch data were judged premature for inclusion in the snow and Tanner crab assessment models, with hybrid-related uncertainty to be handled instead through the existing ABC buffer-setting process.

[[author: state the recommended Tier 4 configuration -- currency, control rule, and buffer -- and the reasoning. Three decisions are open and each moves the OFL materially: (a) the currency. Morphometric maturity gives `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt against `r .f(tier4_by_currency$OFL[tier4_by_currency$currency == ">95 mm"], 2)` kt on >= 95 mm and `r .f(tier4_by_currency$OFL[tier4_by_currency$currency == ">101 mm"], 2)` kt on > 101 mm (Table \@ref(tab:tier4-currencies)). The 2025 assessment recommended >= 95 mm, arguing that morphometric reference points permit the removal of essentially all large males while the trend in large males is firmly negative. That argument has not been answered here; (b) the control rule --- SETTLED (Grant, 2026-08-30): the crab FMP Tier 4 sloped rule, giving F~OFL~ = `r .f(fofl_2026, 4)` at the current status. This is the FMP form and the rule the October 2025 SSC specified for this stock, so it needs no departure argument; the flat alternative is reported as the sensitivity; (c) the buffer. See the ABC section.]]

[[author: the September 2026 meeting notes call for a discussion of author priorities against SSC priorities and where they diverge. The male-only model (`Model 26.2`) is a first step in that direction and is reported here. State where the author's priorities differ and why.]]

# H. Rebuilding analysis and update

[[author: this section is required both by the SAFE guidelines and by the rebuilding plan itself -- Amendment 53 states that the BSAI Crab Plan Team would report stock status and progress towards the rebuilt level in this document. The September 2025 assessment did not include it, which the SSC noted in October 2025. ]]

## Status of the rebuilding plan

On 19 October 2021 NMFS determined, and notified the Council, that the eastern Bering Sea snow crab stock was overfished, the estimated mature male biomass having fallen below the minimum stock size threshold specified in the fishery management plan. The Council developed a rebuilding plan under section 304(e) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, adopted as **Amendment 53** to the Fishery Management Plan for Bering Sea/Aleutian Islands King and Tanner Crabs and implemented before the start of the 2023/24 fishing season.

The rebuilding analysis set the minimum time to rebuild in the absence of fishing (T~min~) at 6 years, which under the National Standard 1 guidelines sets a maximum time to rebuild (T~max~) of 10 years. **The stock is considered rebuilt when mature male biomass reaches B~MSY~.** Median projections placed rebuilding in 2029 under no fishing, under bycatch only, and under the State harvest strategy, and in 2030 under fishing at the ABC. The 5th inter-simulation percentile is 2027 across all scenarios. The 95th is 2034 under no fishing and under bycatch only; under the State harvest strategy and under fishing at the ABC the upper tail does not rebuild within the projection horizon. If mortality events of the kind observed in 2018--19 recur in roughly one year in seven, the projected rebuilding time under no fishing extends to 2034; under the State harvest strategy and under fishing at the ABC the stock does not rebuild within the projection horizon on that scenario. The analysis concluded that the main driver of the rate of rebuilding is recruitment and the ecosystem conditions that permit it, rather than fishing mortality.

## Relationship to previous rebuilding plans

This is the third rebuilding plan for the stock. Snow crab was first declared overfished on 24 September 1999, and a rebuilding plan was adopted as Amendment 14 in 2000. The Amendment 53 environmental assessment's reference list cites Amendment 15 for that plan, but the 2000 environmental assessment itself is titled for Amendment 14 (NPFMC, ADF&G and NMFS staff, December 2000), and Amendment 14 is the citation carried here. In 2009 the NMFS Alaska Region notified the Council that the stock would not be rebuilt by the end of that rebuilding period, 2009/10, and that a revised plan was required; Amendment 39 followed. Amendment 53 replaces those earlier provisions, which were removed from the fishery management plan when it was adopted.

## Progress toward rebuilding

[[author: state progress on the basis actually adopted for the specification. The quantities below are from the Tier 4 calculation on the recommended currency and will need to be restated if the currency or the control rule changes.]]

Mature male biomass is estimated at `r .f(mmb_2026, 2)` kt against a B~MSY~ proxy of `r .f(bmsy_2026, 2)` kt, or `r .f(100*status_2026, 0)` percent of the proxy, with a minimum stock size threshold of `r .f(msst_2026, 2)` kt. The stock is therefore above its minimum stock size threshold but has not, on the point estimate, reached the biomass at which it would be considered rebuilt. Accounting for the uncertainty in the random-effects fit (Section F), status is `r .f(status_2026, 3)` with a 95 percent range of `r .f(status_2026_lci, 3)` to `r .f(status_2026_uci, 3)`. The lower end remains above the threshold for an overfished determination; the upper end reaches the rebuilt threshold. On this basis the stock cannot be declared rebuilt, but neither can rebuilding be excluded on the terminal-year estimate alone.

## Recruitment

Because the rebuilding analysis identifies recruitment as the main driver of the rebuilding rate, recruitment is reported here directly. Estimated male recruitment collapsed to 0.088 and 0.065 billion crab in 2018 and 2019, among the lowest in the time series, before rising to 1.65, 2.36 and 4.28 billion in 2020, 2021 and 2022 and settling near 1.0 billion in 2024 and 2025. The mean over the last five years, 2.01 billion, is above the 1982--2019 mean of 1.22 billion.

That comparison should be treated with caution. Terminal-year recruitment is the least well determined quantity in the assessment: the retrospective analysis gives a Mohn's rho for male recruitment of `r .fmt(.rho("standard","recruitment_male"), 2)`, meaning that recent recruitment estimates revise substantially as data accumulate. The apparent post-collapse recruitment pulse is consistent with the survey observing small crab, but its magnitude in the terminal years should not be relied on. [[author: compare against the survey-derived recruit index produced by `04_plot_recruitment_comparison.R` (`plots/recruitment_survey_vs_model.png`), which is not yet included as a numbered figure; the correlation between the model's estimated recruitment and the survey recruit index over the overlapping period is negative, which deserves comment.]]

\newpage

# I. Data gaps and research priorities

Several data and structural issues identified warrant follow-up:

* **Hybrid identification consistency between ADF&G and NMFS.** ADF&G classifies hybrid crab into three categories (opilio-type, bairdi-type, and unspecified) using a hybrid identification key based on eye color, epistome shape, and secondary morphological characteristics. ADF&G and NMFS do not currently agree on the number of secondary characteristics required for a positive hybrid identification, and the unspecified-hybrid category is present in a non-trivial portion of the time series. Resolving identification criteria across agencies and propagating the resulting categorization back through the historical observer time series would improve the hybrid-data products available to the assessment. However, the value add to the snow crab assessment may be minimal given the low percentage of opilio-type hybrids in the data.

* **Apportionment of retained catch between snow crab and hybrids.** Hybrids are currently retained under either the snow-crab or the Tanner-crab IFQ depending on regulatory identification but are not separately tracked in the retained-catch data. ADF&G has indicated it does not yet have a method for partitioning historical retained catch into hybrid versus parent species. Developing such a partitioning would allow the hybrid sensitivity to be explored more fully (presently the retained time series is identical between the hybrid and non-hybrid configurations evaluated in May 2026 because retained catch already contains hybrids).

* **Quality control on early hybrid catch estimates.** The ADF&G hybrid total-catch estimates contain unexpectedly large values in 1997 (~18 kt of legal-male hybrid catch) and 1998 (~15 kt), with high-CPUE pots peppered around the fishery footprint rather than concentrated in obvious hot spots. ADF&G has flagged these years as requiring follow-up before the data should be considered reliable for regular assessment use.

* **Maturity workflow comparison.** The new spatiotemporal maturity workflow produces a much weaker temporal trend in the probability of terminal molt at size than the legacy workflow. Side-by-side documentation of the two workflows, an evaluation of the spatial sample sizes of chela measurements (which are sparse at many stations and many sizes), uncertainty, and quantification of the degrees of freedom consumed by the spatial process would help the CPT and SSC evaluate the two approaches.

* **Source of the multiple optima in the snow crab assessment.** The immature survey index removed the bimodal jitter signal seen in the May 2026 candidate models, but the underlying source of the multiple optima --- six in the author-recommended model this cycle --- is not understood. The jitter attribution in Section E identifies the parameters that most separate the six optima located this cycle, but not why those combinations are alternative solutions. Carrying that through to the correlation structure and to likelihood profiles would clarify whether the immature index solves a real problem or masks it.

* **Reproductive biology of large male snow crab.** As noted in 2024 and 2025 SSC comments, more research is needed on whether small males can and do mate with large females and produce progeny that will be large males under favorable environmental conditions. This question remains the main axis of uncertainty because the fishery cannot exist without large males and large males are at historical lows.

# Auxiliary files

The following files accompany this assessment and are archived with it. All are in the native format of the assessment program.

* `26_snow_update_newmat_plus_group.dat` --- the model data file.
* `snow.ctl` --- the control file, naming the estimated parameters, their bounds and phases.
* `snow.prj` --- the projection file.
* `gmacs.dat` and `gmacs_files_in.dat` --- the run configuration and the file manifest GMACS reads.
* `gmacs.pin` --- the starting parameter vector. For the accepted fit this is the jitter winner's parameter vector rather than a cold start; its provenance is recorded in `jitter/PROMOTION.md`.
* `gmacs` --- the model executable (GMACS 2.20.34, macOS arm64). `gmacs.exe` is the corresponding Windows build.
* The six derived input files that form the interface between the data preparation scripts and the model: `directed_catch.csv`, `bycatch_catch.csv`, `fishery_size_comps.csv`, `survey_size_comps.csv`, `survey_indices.csv` and `male_maturity_ogive.csv`.

```{r model-overview, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}
# All three columns are keyed off the SAME names, so no positional list can
# drift out of step (model_jittered lives in 0-models.R beside the definitions).
# models_present, not model_defs, so a model that has not been built yet is
# absent from the table rather than present as a blank row.
# NO `Updates` column. It held names(models_present) -- the INTERNAL case keys
# ("26.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + new_mat + male_only)"), which
# 0-models.R states must never reach a table or figure. Printing them put the
# join keys in front of the CPT and made this table 16 in wide, the single
# worst overfull box in the document. `Purpose` already says what each model
# changes (fixed 2026-08-29).
model_overview = data.frame(
  Model    = unname(model_shorts[names(models_present)]),
  Type     = unname(model_type[names(models_present)]),
  Jittered = c(Y = "Yes", n = "No")[unname(model_jittered[names(models_present)])],
  Purpose  = unname(model_purpose[names(models_present)]),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
model_overview <- model_overview[order(to_short(names(models_present))), ]
stopifnot("model-overview: Jittered failed to map to Yes/No" =
            !anyNA(model_overview$Jittered))

flextable::flextable(model_overview) |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 9, part = "all") |>
  # Purpose is a sentence, so give it an explicit width and let it wrap rather
  # than letting autofit() set the table's width from the longest sentence.
  flextable::width(j = c("Model", "Type", "Jittered"), width = c(0.95, 0.85, 0.75)) |>
  flextable::width(j = "Purpose", width = 3.7) |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = "Overview of the models presented in the September 2026 assessment, with the type and purpose of each. 'Jittered' records whether a jitter analysis was run for that model this cycle.",
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "model-overview")
  )


```

```{r like-index-tot, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}

extract_likelihoods <- function(path) {
  out_file <- file.path(path, "Gmacsall.out")
  if (!file.exists(out_file)) return(NULL)

  tmp <- readLines(out_file)

  # Pull the Raw_likelihood vector for a labeled sub-block of
  # Likelihoods_by_type_and_fleet (e.g. "Catches", "Index", "Size_composition").
  get_raw <- function(label) {
    hdr <- grep(paste0("^--", label, ": list"), tmp)[1]
    if (is.na(hdr)) return(numeric(0))
    eol_offset <- grep("^>EOL<", tmp[(hdr + 1):length(tmp)])[1]
    block <- tmp[(hdr + 1):(hdr + eol_offset - 1)]
    raw <- block[grep("^Raw_likelihood", block)][1]
    parts <- strsplit(trimws(sub("^Raw_likelihood\\s*:?\\s*", "", raw)), "\\s+")[[1]]
    as.numeric(parts)
  }

  ## Component labels are DERIVED FROM EACH MODEL, not assumed.
  ##
  ## These were fixed vectors of length 4/4/13, applied positionally. GMACS
  ## emits one likelihood per component the model actually has, so the male-only
  ## model -- which has 3 catch, 2 index and 7 size components -- had every value
  ## after the first divergence shifted onto the wrong label, and the table
  ## showed a model with no female population fitting four female components
  ## while its male survey data read as 0.00 (found 2026-08-29).
  ##
  ## The fit summaries carry fleet, sex, type and maturity per series, in the
  ## same order as the likelihood vectors, so build the labels from them. For the
  ## two-sex models this reproduces the previous vectors exactly.
  .block <- function(header, keys) {
    st <- grep(paste0("^", header, ": dataframe"), tmp)[1]
    if (is.na(st)) return(character(0))
    hdr <- strsplit(trimws(tmp[st + 1]), " +")[[1]]
    rows <- character(0)
    for (ln in tmp[(st + 2):length(tmp)]) {
      if (!nzchar(trimws(ln)) || startsWith(ln, ">")) break
      rows <- c(rows, ln)
    }
    if (!length(rows)) return(character(0))
    m <- do.call(rbind, lapply(strsplit(trimws(rows), " +"), function(x) {
      length(x) <- length(hdr); x
    }))
    colnames(m) <- hdr
    if (!all(keys %in% hdr)) return(character(0))
    sig <- apply(m[, keys, drop = FALSE], 1, paste, collapse = "\u001f")
    unique(sig)
  }
  .fleet <- function(x) c(Pot_Fishery = "Pot", Trawl_Bycatch = "Trawl",
                          NMFS_Trawl_1982 = "NMFS 1982",
                          NMFS_Trawl_1989 = "NMFS 1989")[x]
  .sex   <- function(x) c(male = "M", Male = "M", female = "F", Female = "F",
                          Both = "", both = "")[x]

  catch_lbls <- vapply(strsplit(.block("Catch_fit_summary", c("Fleet","Sex","Type")), "\u001f"),
    function(v) {
      if (v[1] == "Trawl_Bycatch") "Catch: Trawl bycatch"
      else sprintf("Catch: %s %s %s", .fleet(v[1]), tolower(v[3]), .sex(v[2]))
    }, character(1))
  index_lbls <- vapply(strsplit(.block("Index_fit_summary", c("Fleet","Sex","Maturity")), "\u001f"),
    function(v) sprintf("Index: %s %s %s", .fleet(v[1]), .sex(v[2]), tolower(v[3])),
    character(1))
  size_lbls <- vapply(strsplit(.block("Size_fit_summary", c("Fleet","Sex","Type","Maturity")), "\u001f"),
    function(v) {
      if (grepl("^NMFS", v[1])) sprintf("Size: %s %s %s", .fleet(v[1]), .sex(v[2]), tolower(v[4]))
      else sprintf("Size: %s %s %s", .fleet(v[1]), .sex(v[2]), tolower(v[3]))
    }, character(1))

  catch_vals <- get_raw("Catches")
  index_vals <- get_raw("Index")
  size_vals  <- get_raw("Size_composition")

  ## If these ever disagree the labels are wrong, which is exactly the failure
  ## this replaced. Fail the knit rather than print a mislabelled table.
  stopifnot(
    "catch likelihoods do not match the catch fit summary" = length(catch_vals) == length(catch_lbls),
    "index likelihoods do not match the index fit summary" = length(index_vals) == length(index_lbls),
    "size likelihoods do not match the size fit summary"   = length(size_vals)  == length(size_lbls))

  # Other components (SRR, Tag, Growth, Penalties, Priors, ...) still come from
  # the aggregate Likelihoods_by_type block.
  st  <- grep("^Likelihoods_by_type: list", tmp)[1]
  eol_offset <- grep("^>EOL<", tmp[(st + 1):length(tmp)])[1]
  rows <- tmp[(st + 1):(st + eol_offset - 1)]
  clean_rows <- gsub(":", "", rows)
  parts <- strsplit(trimws(clean_rows), " +")
  vals <- sapply(parts, function(x) as.numeric(tail(x, 1)))
  names(vals) <- sapply(parts, function(x) x[1])

  other_keys <- c("Stock_recruitment", "Tagging_data", "Growth_data",
                  "Penalties", "Priors", "Positive_growth_penalty",
                  "Total", "Initial_size_structure")
  other_lbls <- c("SRR", "Tag", "Growth", "Penalties", "Priors",
                  "Positive_growth_penalty", "Total", "Initial_size_structure")
  other_vals <- unname(vals[other_keys])

  dat <- data.frame(
    Object = c(catch_lbls, index_lbls, size_lbls, other_lbls),
    Value  = c(catch_vals, index_vals, size_vals, other_vals)
  )
  colnames(dat)[2] <- path
  return(dat)
}

# models_present, not model_defs: a model that has not been built is absent
# from the table rather than present as a blank column.
tot_likes <- lapply(models_present, extract_likelihoods)

# extract_likelihoods() returns NULL when a model directory has no Gmacsall.out
# -- a fit that never finished writing, not a missing folder, so the dir.exists()
# guard above does not catch it. Left to purrr::reduce() that surfaces as
# `auto_copy(): x and y must share the same src ... y is NULL`, which names
# neither the chunk's real problem nor the model. Name it instead. Hit
# 2026-08-28: Model 26.1a had a complete fit but no Gmacsall.out, and it killed
# the whole render at chunk 18 of 93.
.bad <- names(models_present)[vapply(tot_likes, is.null, logical(1))]
if (length(.bad))
  stop("No Gmacsall.out for: ", paste(to_short(.bad), collapse = ", "),
       ". Re-fit the model, or run gmacs -binp gmacs.bar -hess_step 5 in its ",
       "directory to regenerate the outputs from the existing MLE.")

tot_likes <- tot_likes %>% purrr::reduce(dplyr::full_join)

# NA here means the model HAS NO SUCH COMPONENT (the male-only model has no
# female data), which is not the same as a component that was fitted and
# contributed zero. Filling with 0 conflated the two. Left as NA and rendered as
# a dash by the three table chunks below (2026-08-29).
rownames(tot_likes) <- tot_likes$Object
tot_likes <- tot_likes[,-1]
colnames(tot_likes) <- as.character(to_short(names(models_present)))
# Columns in model-number order, not folder order. models_present follows the
# directory listing, which since the 26.x renumbering puts the male-only model
# (26.2) ahead of the 2019 diagnostic (26.1c). model_order is defined once in
# 0-models.R and is what to_short() already uses for factor levels.
tot_likes <- tot_likes[, intersect(model_order, colnames(tot_likes)), drop = FALSE]

# Render with flextable so the caption produces a Word bookmark/sequence
# field that bookdown's \@ref(tab:like-comp-tot) can resolve. Transposed so
# that models are rows and likelihood components are columns to better fit
# the landscape page.
tot_likes_t <- as.data.frame(t(signif(tot_likes, 5)), check.names = FALSE)
tot_likes_df <- data.frame(
  Model       = rownames(tot_likes_t),
  tot_likes_t,
  check.names = FALSE
)

# Diagnostic dump of the likelihood components, one file per knit date. Nothing
# reads it back -- it exists so the components can be diffed between renders.
# Written to data/diagnostics/, not the repo root: the root is off limits, and
# data/derived/ is the six-file model interface, which this is not part of.
dir.create("data/diagnostics", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
write.csv(tot_likes_t,
          file = file.path("data/diagnostics",
                           paste0("likelihood_components_", Sys.Date(), ".csv")))

# Components in ROWS, models in COLUMNS -- see the note in the composition
# chunk. Six models is a comfortable number of columns; eight long component
# names is not. The "Catch: "/"Index: " prefixes are the slicing keys and are
# kept in the row labels, where there is room for them.
.keep <- grepl("^(Catch|Index): ", rownames(tot_likes))
index_and_catch <- tot_likes[.keep, , drop = FALSE]
index_and_catch <- as.data.frame(lapply(index_and_catch, round, 2),
                                 check.names = FALSE)
index_and_catch <- cbind(
  data.frame(Component = rownames(tot_likes)[.keep], check.names = FALSE),
  index_and_catch)
rownames(index_and_catch) <- NULL

flextable::flextable(index_and_catch) |>
  # A dash marks a component the model does not have (see the NA note above);
  # it is not a fitted value of zero.
  flextable::colformat_double(na_str = "\u2013") |>
  # fontsize BEFORE autofit: autofit() measures the text at the CURRENT size, so
  # shrinking the font afterwards leaves the old, wider column widths in place.
  # set_table_properties(width=) does NOT constrain width in flextable 0.10.0 --
  # measured, it left these tables 13-22 in wide (2026-08-29).
  flextable::fontsize(size = 7, part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = "Catch and index likelihood components (negative log-likelihood, dimensionless), one row per component and one column per model. Row labels name the fleet and, where it applies, the sex: M is male, F is female. The two survey rows are the 1982-1988 and 1989-present selectivity eras.",
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "like-index-tot")
  )


```

```{r like-comp-tot, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}
# Components in ROWS, models in COLUMNS -- the opposite of the other two
# likelihood tables. There are thirteen size-composition components and only six
# models, so models-as-rows put thirteen long headers across the page and the
# table measured 22 in wide. tot_likes is already component-by-model.
comp_like <- tot_likes[grepl("^Size: ", rownames(tot_likes)), , drop = FALSE]
comp_like <- as.data.frame(lapply(comp_like, function(x) signif(x, 4)),
                           check.names = FALSE)
rownames(comp_like) <- sub("^Size: ", "", rownames(tot_likes)[grepl("^Size: ", rownames(tot_likes))])
comp_like <- cbind(data.frame(Component = rownames(comp_like), check.names = FALSE),
                   comp_like)
rownames(comp_like) <- NULL

flextable::flextable(comp_like) |>
  # A dash marks a component the model does not have (see the NA note above);
  # it is not a fitted value of zero.
  flextable::colformat_double(na_str = "\u2013") |>
  # fontsize BEFORE autofit: autofit() measures the text at the CURRENT size, so
  # shrinking the font afterwards leaves the old, wider column widths in place.
  # set_table_properties(width=) does NOT constrain width in flextable 0.10.0 --
  # measured, it left these tables 13-22 in wide (2026-08-29).
  flextable::fontsize(size = 7, part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = "Size-composition likelihood components (negative log-likelihood, dimensionless), one row per component and one column per model. Row labels name the fleet, the survey era where it applies (NMFS 1982 is 1982-1988 and NMFS 1989 is 1989-present), the sex (M male, F female) and the maturity state.",
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "like-comp-tot")
  )

```{r like-other-tot, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}
# Components in ROWS, models in COLUMNS, as in the other two likelihood tables.
.keep <- !grepl("^(Size|Catch|Index): ", rownames(tot_likes))
other_like <- tot_likes[.keep, , drop = FALSE]
other_like <- as.data.frame(lapply(other_like, function(x) signif(x, 4)),
                            check.names = FALSE)
other_like <- cbind(
  data.frame(Component = gsub("_", " ", rownames(tot_likes)[.keep]),
             check.names = FALSE),
  other_like)
rownames(other_like) <- NULL

flextable::flextable(other_like) |>
  # A dash marks a component the model does not have (see the NA note above);
  # it is not a fitted value of zero.
  flextable::colformat_double(na_str = "\u2013") |>
  # fontsize BEFORE autofit: autofit() measures the text at the CURRENT size, so
  # shrinking the font afterwards leaves the old, wider column widths in place.
  # set_table_properties(width=) does NOT constrain width in flextable 0.10.0 --
  # measured, it left these tables 13-22 in wide (2026-08-29).
  flextable::fontsize(size = 7, part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = "Remaining likelihood components (negative log-likelihood, dimensionless), one row per component and one column per model. These are the penalties, priors and data components that are not catch, index or size composition. Note that Model 25.3 was fitted under GMACS 2.20.22, which reports the growth-increment likelihood in the Tagging row; every model fitted under 2.20.34 reports it in the Growth row and carries zero for Tagging. The two are the same quantity under different version names -- Model 25.3's 7965.08 and Model 26.1's 7970.26 are the same fit to the same growth data -- and the row should not be read as Model 25.3 having a tagging likelihood the others lack. The fall to about 4881 from Model 26.1a onward is the correction of the growth transcription error, not a change of component.",
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "like-other-tot")
  )

```{r max-grad, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}

## Turn a GMACS parameter name into something a reader can act on.
## "T_pars_est[3]" says nothing; the descriptive name GMACS carries for the same
## parameter is "Log(Rbar)". Expand the leading token and drop the underscores.
.pretty_par <- function(x) {
  if (is.na(x)) return(NA_character_)
  x <- sub("^Log\\(Rbar\\)$",     "log mean recruitment", x)
  x <- sub("^Log\\(R0\\)$",       "log unfished recruitment", x)
  x <- sub("^Log\\(Rinitial\\)$", "log initial recruitment", x)
  x <- sub("^Log\\((.*)\\)$",     "log \\1", x)
  x <- sub("^M_base_",  "base natural mortality, ", x)
  x <- sub("^M_",       "natural mortality, ", x)
  x <- sub("^Sel_",     "selectivity, ", x)
  x <- sub("^Initial_logN_for_sex_", "initial numbers at size, ", x)
  x <- sub("^Rec_",     "recruitment, ", x)
  x <- gsub("_", " ", x)
  x <- sub("block group 1 block ", "block ", x)
  x
}

extract_max_gradient <- function(path) {
  grad_file <- file.path(path, "gradient.dat")
  if (!file.exists(grad_file)) {
    return(data.frame(NPar = NA_integer_, Parameter = NA_character_,
                      Description = NA_character_, MaxAbsGradient = NA_real_))
  }
  grad <- read.table(grad_file, header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  idx <- which.max(abs(grad$Gradient))

  ## GMACS's own descriptive name for the same parameter. The "--Estimated
  ## parameters" block of Gmacsall.out lists every parameter with a trailing
  ## index that counts only the ESTIMATED ones, and that index is the row number
  ## in gradient.dat -- verified 2026-08-29: 412 estimated parameters against 412
  ## gradient rows, with M_pars_est[15] resolving to
  ## M_female_immature_block_group_1_block_2, the parameter the convergence
  ## section discusses.
  desc <- NA_character_
  out_file <- file.path(path, "Gmacsall.out")
  if (file.exists(out_file)) {
    tmp <- readLines(out_file, warn = FALSE)
    st  <- grep("^--Estimated parameters: dataframe", tmp)[1]
    if (!is.na(st)) {
      for (ln in tmp[(st + 2):length(tmp)]) {
        if (!nzchar(trimws(ln)) || startsWith(ln, ">")) break
        f <- strsplit(trimws(ln), " +")[[1]]
        if (length(f) >= 11 && suppressWarnings(!is.na(as.integer(tail(f, 1)))) &&
            as.integer(tail(f, 1)) == idx) { desc <- sub(":$", "", f[2]); break }
      }
    }
  }

  data.frame(
    NPar           = nrow(grad),
    Parameter      = grad$ParName[idx],
    Description    = .pretty_par(desc),
    MaxAbsGradient = abs(grad$Gradient[idx])
  )
}

# models_present, not model_defs: extract_max_gradient() returns an all-NA row
# for a folder that does not exist, which would render as a blank row here.
gradlist <- list()
for(i in seq_along(models_present)){

  out <- extract_max_gradient(models_present[i])
 gradlist[[i]] <- data.frame(
    Model          = to_short(names(models_present)[i]),
    NPar           = out$NPar,
    Parameter      = out$Parameter,
    Description    = out$Description,
    MaxAbsGradient = round(out$MaxAbsGradient, 5)
  )
}
max_grad_df <- do.call("rbind", gradlist)
# Rows in model-number order. gradlist follows models_present, i.e. folder order,
# which since the 26.x renumbering puts 26.2 ahead of 26.1c and disagreed with
# every other table in the document (2026-08-29).
max_grad_df <- max_grad_df[order(max_grad_df$Model), ]

colnames(max_grad_df) <- c("Model", "N parameters", "Parameter", "What it is", "Max |gradient|")

flextable::flextable(max_grad_df) |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = "Maximum absolute gradient (dimensionless) for each model, and the parameter carrying it. The Parameter column gives GMACS's internal name and \"What it is\" the quantity that name refers to: the T_pars (theta) block holds the recruitment scale and the initial numbers at size, M_pars natural mortality, S_pars selectivity and G_pars growth. A gradient of zero is the result of the Newton polishing described in the text; Model 25.3 could not be polished and is reported as originally fitted.",
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "max-grad")
  )

```{r obscatch, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}
# 1. Extract and combine data from multiple cases
catch_comparison <- case_for_data_table %>%
  purrr::map_dfr(function(case_name) {
    reslst$repsLst[[case_name]]$Catch_fit_summary %>%
      dplyr::transmute(
        Model = case_name,
        Year = as.numeric(year),
        # Create descriptive labels for the catch categories
        Category = dplyr::case_when(
          type == "retained" ~ "Retained (kt)",
          type == "discarded" & sex == "female" ~ "Discard Female",
          type == "discarded" & sex == "male" & fleet == "Pot_Fishery" ~ "Discard Male Pot",
          fleet == "Trawl_Bycatch" ~ "Non-directed Bycatch",
          TRUE ~ paste(type, sex, fleet)
        ),
        obs = as.numeric(obs)
      )
  })

# 2. Pivot so each catch category appears once per model.
# The two models in case_for_data_table are the 2025 rolled-forward reference and
# the author-recommended model. Until 2026-08-29 this block labeled the SECOND of
# them " + hybrids" -- a survival from the May bracket, where the pair really was
# base vs hybrid. Neither September model contains hybrid data, so the table was
# presenting the recommended model's discards to the reader as a hybrid run. The
# columns are now labeled with the models' own shortnames, which is also what
# makes the table informative: it shows how the observed catch inputs changed
# between the 2025 assessment and this one.
PlotTab <- catch_comparison %>%
  mutate(Model = as.character(to_short(Model))) %>%
  # Retained catch and non-directed bycatch are the same series in both models
  # for every year the earlier model covers, so carry them once, from the
  # recommended model, which also supplies the terminal year.
  dplyr::filter(!(Model == to_short(case_for_data_table[1]) &
                    Category %in% c("Retained (kt)", "Non-directed Bycatch"))) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from  = c(Category, Model),
    values_from = obs,
    names_sep   = ", "
  ) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(Year)

# A gap after the pivot means one of two different things, and they must not be
# printed the same way. Inside a model's own year span it means the fishery took
# nothing -- the 2022 and 2023 closures -- and belongs in the table as 0. Outside
# it, the model simply does not extend that far: Model 25.3 ends in 2024, so its
# 2025 cells are not zero catch, they are no data. A blanket is.na() <- 0 printed
# 0.00 for both (fixed 2026-08-29).
.span <- vapply(case_for_data_table, function(cs)
  max(as.numeric(reslst$repsLst[[cs]]$Catch_fit_summary$year), na.rm = TRUE),
  numeric(1))
names(.span) <- as.character(to_short(case_for_data_table))
for (nm in setdiff(names(PlotTab), "Year")) {
  .mdl <- sub("^.*, ", "", nm)                     # "" for the shared columns
  .end <- if (.mdl %in% names(.span)) .span[[.mdl]] else max(.span)
  .fill <- is.na(PlotTab[[nm]]) & PlotTab$Year <= .end
  PlotTab[[nm]][.fill] <- 0
}

# Retained catch and non-directed bycatch come from one model only, so drop the
# model suffix from those two columns; the four discard columns keep theirs.
.acc <- as.character(to_short(case_for_data_table[2]))
names(PlotTab)[names(PlotTab) == paste0("Retained (kt), ", .acc)]        <- "Retained"
names(PlotTab)[names(PlotTab) == paste0("Non-directed Bycatch, ", .acc)] <- "Non-directed bycatch"

# Column order: the shared series first, then each discard series with the
# reference model beside the recommended one.
.want <- c("Year", "Retained", "Non-directed bycatch",
           paste0("Discard Male Pot, ",   as.character(to_short(case_for_data_table))),
           paste0("Discard Female, ",     as.character(to_short(case_for_data_table))))
stopifnot("obscatch: expected columns are missing" = all(.want %in% names(PlotTab)))
PlotTab <- PlotTab[, .want]

# Compact headers. The table is 44 crab years, so it wants to stay PORTRAIT --
# landscape buys width but costs height and pushed it from two pages to three,
# which duplicated its caption a second time. Shortening the headers instead
# keeps it inside the portrait line width. The models are named in the caption.
names(PlotTab) <- sub("^Discard Male Pot, Model ",   "Male disc. ",   names(PlotTab))
names(PlotTab) <- sub("^Discard Female, Model ",     "Female disc. ", names(PlotTab))
names(PlotTab)[names(PlotTab) == "Non-directed bycatch"] <- "Bycatch"

# 3. Render with flextable + run_autonum so the Word caption carries a SEQ
#    field that \@ref(tab:obscatch) can target. Year is an integer, not a
#    measurement: colformat_int() stops flextable printing it as "1,982".
# Year must be an integer column before it reaches flextable. As a double it
# slips past colformat_int() and is then caught by colformat_double(), which
# printed the crab year as "2,013.00" (fixed 2026-08-29). Restrict the double
# formatter to the catch columns for the same reason.
PlotTab$Year <- as.integer(PlotTab$Year)
.numcols <- setdiff(names(PlotTab), "Year")

flextable::flextable(PlotTab) |>
  # 44 crab years, so this table always breaks across pages. flextable repeats
  # the caption in the longtable continuation head, which repeats the \label
  # with it and makes \@ref(tab:obscatch) ambiguous; caption_repeat = FALSE
  # keeps the caption (and the label) on the first page only (2026-08-29).
  flextable::set_table_properties(opts_pdf = list(caption_repeat = FALSE)) |>
  flextable::colformat_int(j = "Year", big.mark = "") |>
  flextable::colformat_double(j = .numcols, digits = 2, na_str = "–") |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 8, part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = paste0(
      "Observed catch used in the assessment (1,000 t), by crab year. Retained ",
      "catch and non-directed bycatch are common to both models. Male and female ",
      "pot-fishery discards are shown for ", as.character(to_short(case_for_data_table[1])),
      " and ", as.character(to_short(case_for_data_table[2])),
      ", so that the effect of the revised ADF&G delivery on the discard series ",
      "is visible; the two models are otherwise fit to the same removals. A zero ",
      "is no catch -- the directed fishery was closed in 2022 and 2023 -- while a ",
      "dash means the model's data do not extend to that year."),
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "obscatch")
  )

```{r stepchange, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}
# Define the target management parameters to extract
# We map the GMACS label to the column index based on your logic:
# BMSY, Status, FMSY usually in index 3; FOFL, OFL in index 4.
mgmt_targets <- list(
  "BMSY"   = 3,
  "Bcurr/BMSY" = 3,
  "Fmsy"   = 4,
  "Fofl"   = 4,
  "OFL"    = 3
)

# Helper function to extract management quantities from one model folder
extract_mgmt_quantities <- function(path, model_name) {
  out_file <- file.path(path, "Gmacsall.out")
  if (!file.exists(out_file)) return(NULL)

  tmp <- readLines(out_file)

  # Identify the summary block
  st  <- grep("BMSY", tmp)[1]
  end <- grep("Ofl", tmp) |> tail(1)
  mgmt_block <- tmp[st:end]

  # Extract values based on targets
  values <- lapply(names(mgmt_targets), function(target) {
    line <- mgmt_block[grep(target, mgmt_block)][1]
    if (is.na(line)) return(NA)

    # Split by one or more spaces
    parts <- unlist(strsplit(trimws(line), " "))
    idx   <- mgmt_targets[[target]]
    return(as.numeric(parts[idx]))
  })

  names(values) <- names(mgmt_targets)

  # Extract male natural mortality (immature and mature) for the most recent
  # year. M is constant across the 22 size classes, so the first size-class
  # column is sufficient.
  m_start <- grep("Natural_mortality-by-class: dataframe", tmp, fixed = TRUE)[1]
  m_imm <- NA_real_
  m_mat <- NA_real_
  if (!is.na(m_start)) {
    eod_rel <- grep(">EOD<", tmp[(m_start + 1):length(tmp)], fixed = TRUE)[1]
    m_end <- m_start + eod_rel - 1          # last DATA line, EOD is m_start + eod_rel
    # Was (m_end - 1), which dropped that last data line. In a two-sex model the
    # dropped row is the terminal year's immature FEMALE, so the male lookup
    # below still found what it wanted and the bug was invisible; in the
    # male-only model it is the terminal immature MALE, and the table rendered a
    # silent NA for M (imm males). Fixed 2026-08-29.
    m_block <- tmp[(m_start + 2):m_end]
    m_df <- utils::read.table(text = m_block, header = FALSE,
                              stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    colnames(m_df)[1:4] <- c("Year", "Sex", "Maturity", "M")
    males <- m_df[m_df$Sex == "male", ]
    latest <- max(males$Year, na.rm = TRUE)
    m_imm <- males$M[males$Year == latest & males$Maturity == "immature"][1]
    m_mat <- males$M[males$Year == latest & males$Maturity == "mature"][1]
  }
  values[["M (imm males)"]] <- as.numeric(m_imm)
  values[["M (mat males)"]] <- as.numeric(m_mat)

  # Terminal-year MMB and average recruitment. The checklist requires both in
  # this table and the caption already described them, but neither was extracted
  # (added 2026-08-29).
  #
  # MMB is the SSB column of the Overall_summary block in its last year. That it
  # is biomass at MATING, not at the survey, is not merely assumed: Model 25.3's
  # terminal value, 137.4593369, is identical to the 2024 entry of the 2025
  # vintage in data/historical/historical_mmb_mating_by_assessment.csv.
  #
  # Average recruitment is GMACS's own `Male Spr_rbar`, i.e. the mean male
  # recruitment over the window the SPR reference points are computed on, so it
  # is the average that belongs beside B_MSY rather than one recomputed here.
  s_start <- grep("^Summary: dataframe", tmp)[1]
  term_yr <- NA_real_; mmb_term <- NA_real_
  if (!is.na(s_start)) {
    s_rows <- character(0)
    for (ln in tmp[(s_start + 2):length(tmp)]) {
      if (!nzchar(trimws(ln)) || startsWith(ln, ">")) break
      s_rows <- c(s_rows, ln)
    }
    if (length(s_rows)) {
      last <- strsplit(trimws(tail(s_rows, 1)), " +")[[1]]
      term_yr  <- as.numeric(last[1])
      mmb_term <- as.numeric(last[2])
    }
  }
  rbar_line <- grep("^Male Spr_rbar", tmp, value = TRUE)[1]
  rbar <- if (is.na(rbar_line)) NA_real_ else
    as.numeric(strsplit(trimws(rbar_line), " +")[[1]][4]) / 1e6

  values[["Terminal year"]]  <- term_yr
  values[["MMB (terminal)"]] <- mmb_term
  values[["Avg recruitment"]] <- rbar

  return(dplyr::as_tibble(values) |> dplyr::mutate(Model = model_name))
}

# Iterate over the models this cycle ran, not the retained May bracket -- this is
# the table the OFL/BMSY comparison is read from, so a row per non-existent model
# would put NA management quantities in front of the CPT.
ref_table <- names(models_present) |>
  purrr::map_dfr(~extract_mgmt_quantities(models_present[.x], .x)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Model = to_short(Model)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(Model) |>          # model_order, not folder order (0-models.R)
  dplyr::select(Model, everything()) # Reorder to put Model first

# Render with flextable so \@ref(tab:stepchange) resolves in Word output.
# Terminal year is a year, not a measurement. Left as a double it is caught by
# colformat_double() and printed "2,024.00", so make it an integer and keep the
# double formatter off it -- the same trap as the Year column of Table
# \@ref(tab:obscatch).
ref_table$`Terminal year` <- as.integer(ref_table$`Terminal year`)

flextable::flextable(ref_table) |>
  flextable::colformat_int(j = "Terminal year", big.mark = "") |>
  flextable::colformat_double(j = setdiff(names(ref_table), c("Model", "Terminal year")),
                              digits = 2) |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 7, part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = "Management quantities by model, derived from maximum likelihood estimates using Tier 3 reference points. Biomass and OFL in 1,000 t; natural mortality per year; average recruitment in billions of crab. Reported natural mortality is for immature and mature males in the terminal year of each model. Note that Model 26.1c terminates in 2019, which is itself a mortality-event year, so its M is an event value and not comparable with the post-event values reported for the other models. MMB is mature male biomass at mating in that terminal year, which differs across models and is given alongside it; status is Bcurr/BMSY, in which Bcurr is the projected mature male biomass the control rule acts on. Average recruitment is GMACS's Spr_rbar for males, the mean over the window the spawning-biomass-per-recruit reference points are computed on. [[author: the Fmsy and Fofl columns are GMACS's fleet-1 values and are not on the scale of an annual instantaneous fishing mortality -- the 2025 assessment reported the same quantity the same way (34.37 for the model carried here as 25.3). Confirm what they are and relabel or convert before this goes to the CPT.]]",
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "stepchange")
  )

# --- 1. Extract Weight and Results ---
# Direct indexing instead of eval(parse)
rep_obj     <- reslst$repsLst[[names(report_model)]]
weight_data <- rep_obj$IndivWeightByXM

# Extract weight-at-length vectors (assuming 22 size classes)
male_wt   <- weight_data |> 
  dplyr::filter(Sex == "male", Year == 1982, Maturity == 'mature') |> 
  dplyr::select(matches("^[0-9]")) |> as.numeric()

female_wt <- weight_data |> 
  dplyr::filter(Sex == "female", Year == 1982, Maturity == 'mature') |> 
  dplyr::select(matches("^[0-9]")) |> as.numeric()

# --- 2. Extract Population Numbers (N) ---
# Helper to extract dataframe sections from Gmacsall.out without manual loops
extract_gmacs_df <- function(lines, header) {
  start <- grep(header, lines, fixed = TRUE) + 1
  end   <- grep("EOD", lines[start:length(lines)])[1] + start - 2
  read.table(text = lines[start:end])
}

gmacs_lines <- readLines(file.path(report_model, "/Gmacsall.out"))
n_males_mat <- extract_gmacs_df(gmacs_lines, "N(males_mature): dataframe")
n_females_mat <- extract_gmacs_df(gmacs_lines, "N(females_mature): dataframe")

# --- 3. Extract Selectivity ---
dfrSel <- wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "selfcns") |> 
  dplyr::filter(type == "capture", fleet == "NMFS_Trawl_1989", 
                case == names(report_model), sex == 'male', year == 2023)

# Ensure selectivity vector length matches size classes (22)
male_sel <- dfrSel |> 
  dplyr::select(matches("^[0-9]")) |> as.numeric()

# --- 4. Define Size Filters ---
# Logic for biomass/abundance tiers based on carapace width (CW)
sizes <- seq(27.5, 132.5, 5)
mask_95  <- ifelse(sizes >= 95, 1.0, 0.0)

# User-specific logic for >105mm: 
# Includes 50% of the 97.5 bin
# Standardizing to the logic in your snippet:
mask_101 <- dplyr::case_when(
  sizes > 105  ~ 1.0,
  sizes == 102.5 ~ 0.5, 
  TRUE         ~ 0.0
)


midpoints <- seq(27.5, 132.5, by = 5)

# --- 5. Vectorized Calculations ---
# Convert N dataframes to matrices (excluding Year column)
mat_males   <- as.matrix(n_males_mat[-1, -1])
mat_females <- as.matrix(n_females_mat[-1, -1])

# Calculate Biomass and Abundance (in 1,000 t or billions)
results_tab <- data.frame(
  Year = n_males_mat[-1, 1],
  MMB_95   = (mat_males %*% (male_wt * male_sel * mask_95)) / 1e6,
  MMB_101  = (mat_males %*% (male_wt * male_sel * mask_101)) / 1e6,
  Abund_101 = (mat_males %*% (male_sel * mask_101)) / 1e3,
  # Population (True Values)
  FMB_tot      = (mat_females %*% female_wt) / 1e6,
  MMB_tot      = (mat_males %*% male_wt) / 1e6,
  MMB_95_tot   = (mat_males %*% (male_wt * mask_95)) / 1e6,
  MMB_101_tot  = (mat_males %*% (male_wt * mask_101)) / 1e6,
  Abund_101_tot = (mat_males %*% mask_101) / 1e3
)

survey_results <- data.frame(
  # Predicted (Subject to Survey Selectivity)
  Year      = wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Index_fit_summary") |> 
    filter(sex == 'female', case == names(report_model)) |> pull(year),
  FMB      = wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Index_fit_summary") |> 
    filter(sex == 'female', case == names(report_model)) |> pull(prd),
  MMB      = wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Index_fit_summary") |> 
    filter(sex == 'male', case == names(report_model)) |> pull(prd)
)

# --- 6. Final Table Formatting ---
PlotTab <- survey_results |> 
  full_join(results_tab) |> 
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) |>
  mutate(across(-Year, ~round(.x, 2))) %>%
  select(Year, FMB, MMB, MMB_95, MMB_101, Abund_101, FMB_tot, MMB_tot, MMB_95_tot, MMB_101_tot, Abund_101_tot) %>%
  arrange(Year)

pander::pander(
  PlotTab,
  split.cells = 10,
  split.table = Inf,
  caption = "\\label{predsurvbio}Maximum likelihood estimates of mature male (MMB) and female (FMB) biomass. Columns 2-6 are subject to survey selectivity; columns 7-11 are population values."
)

```



```{r predtotnum, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval = FALSE}
# --- 0. Helper + load Gmacsall.out ---
# Inlined here so this chunk does not depend on the eval=FALSE chunk above.
extract_gmacs_df <- function(lines, header) {
  start <- grep(header, lines, fixed = TRUE) + 1
  end   <- grep("EOD", lines[start:length(lines)])[1] + start - 2
  read.table(text = lines[start:end])
}

gmacs_lines <- readLines(file.path(report_model, "/Gmacsall.out"))

# --- 1. Extract Data Using Helper ---
n_males   <- extract_gmacs_df(gmacs_lines, "N(males): dataframe")
n_females <- extract_gmacs_df(gmacs_lines, "N(females): dataframe")

# --- 2. Vectorized Calculation ---
# Convert to matrices and drop the first two metadata columns (Year, Season)
mat_m <- as.matrix(n_males[-1, -1])
mat_f <- as.matrix(n_females[-1, -1])

# Calculate row sums for both matrices and convert to billions
# (Assumes model units are in thousands)
total_n_billions <- (rowSums(mat_m) + rowSums(mat_f)) / 1e6

# --- 3. Final Table Assembly ---
tmp_mat <- data.frame(
  `Survey year`   = n_males[-1, 1],
  `Total numbers` = round(total_n_billions, 2),
  check.names     = FALSE
)

# --- 4. Render Table (kable for bookdown table cross-references in Word) ---
knitr::kable(
  tmp_mat,
  caption = "(\\#tab:predtotnum) Maximum likelihood estimates of total numbers of crab (billions), not subject to survey selectivity at the time of the survey."
)

```



```{r,echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE,message=F, eval = FALSE}

# --- 1. Extract Summary Data for all targeted cases ---
# extractRep1Results returns a tidy dataframe containing 'case'
summary_all <- wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Summary") |> 
  dplyr::filter(case %in% case_for_data_table) |> 
  dplyr::select(case, year, SSB, rec_male) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

# --- 2. Extract Fishing Mortality for all targeted cases ---
# We loop through the case vector to pull the internal list objects
fm_all <- case_for_data_table |> 
  purrr::map_dfr(function(c_name) {
    rep_obj <- reslst$repsLst[[c_name]]
    
    # Identify the correct dataframe name for this specific model
    # Checks for "capture_rate" first, then "FM"
    f_df_name <- intersect(names(rep_obj), 
                           c("Fully-selected_capture_rate_by_season_sex_and_fishery", 
                             "Fully-selected_FM_by_season_sex_and_fishery"))[1]
    
    if (is.na(f_df_name)) {
      message("Warning: No F-mortality data found for case: ", c_name)
      return(NULL)
    }
    
    rep_obj[[f_df_name]] |> 
      dplyr::filter(sex == 'male', fleet == "Pot_Fishery") |> 
      dplyr::transmute(
        case = c_name,
        year = as.numeric(year),
        f_mort = as.numeric(`2`) # Directed fishing season
      )
  })

# --- 3. Join and Format for Comparison ---
# Use a join to ensure the FM and MMB align correctly for every model
sum_mat <- summary_all |>
  dplyr::inner_join(fm_all, by = c("case", "year")) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Model                 = as.character(to_short(case)),
    `Survey Year`         = year,
    `Mature Male Biomass` = round(as.numeric(SSB), 2),
    `Male Recruits`       = round(as.numeric(rec_male) / 1e6, 2), # Billions
    `Fishing Mortality`   = round(f_mort, 2)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(Model, `Survey Year`)

# --- 4. Render Table ---
pander::pander(
  sum_mat,
  split.cells = 10,
  caption = "\\label{predsurvbio_tot} Comparison of mature male biomass (MMB) at mating, male recruitment (billions), and fully-selected fishing mortality ($F$) across selected models."
)

```

```{r surveyplots, echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, width = 12, height = 7, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Observed male survey biomass for models across hybrid and maturity workflow scenarios."}
dfrIndxFit_plot <- wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Index_fit_summary")  %>%
  dplyr::filter(case %in% c("25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + imm_surv)", # base
                            "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + hyb_surv)", # base + hybrid
                            "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + new_mat + imm_surv)", # base with newmat
                            "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + hyb_both + new_mat)") & # base + hybrid + newmat
             sex == "male" )   %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Categorize index
    Index_category = case_when(
      case == "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + imm_surv)" ~ "Base",
      case ==  "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + hyb_surv)" ~ "Base + hybrid",
      case ==  "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + new_mat + imm_surv)" ~ "Base + newmat",
      case ==  "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + hyb_both + new_mat)" ~ "Base + hybrid + newmat",
      .default = NA
    )) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    
    # Confidence interval calculations
    sd_log = sqrt(log(1 + as.numeric(actual_CV)^2)),
    obs = as.numeric(obs),
    lba    = qlnorm(0.05, log(obs), sd_log),
    uba    = qlnorm(0.95, log(obs), sd_log),
    year = as.numeric(year)
  )

# --- Generate the 4-Panel Plot ---
p_idx_final <- ggplot() +
  # Observations (Single black error bar per year/sex/panel)
  geom_errorbar(
    data = dfrIndxFit_plot,
    aes(x = year, ymin = lba, ymax = uba, color = Index_category), 
    width = 0.3, 
    position = position_dodge(width=0.5),
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  # Observations (Single black point per year/sex/panel)
  geom_point(
    data = dfrIndxFit_plot,
    position = position_dodge(width=0.5),
    aes(x = year, y = obs, color = Index_category), 
    size = 1.2
  ) +
  # Formatting and Scales
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(
    x = "Year", 
    y = "NMFS Survey Biomass (1,000 t)",
    color = "Scenario",
    subtitle = "Points/Bars: Shared Observations",
    caption = "Error bars represent 95% log-normal confidence intervals on observations."
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  facet_wrap(~maturity, ncol = 1) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )

print(p_idx_final)
```
