One rung of this sweep carries no additional survey information. The peels withhold the survey through `END_YEAR` minus the peel count, so peel five ends the survey in 2020 and peel six in 2019; the 2020 survey was cancelled, and the two peels are therefore fit to the same survey series and differ only in the fishery years GMACS truncates. Their data files are byte-identical. The step between those two points on the figure should not be read as the effect of removing a survey year.

```{r rema-fit, echo=FALSE, out.width="72%", fig.cap="Random-effects (REMA) fit to the survey biomass series for each of the three Tier 4 currencies -- morphometrically mature males (top), males >= 95 mm (middle) and males > 101 mm (bottom). Points are the survey observations with their sampling intervals; the line and shaded band are the smoothed series and its 95 percent prediction interval. The smoothed terminal value is the biomass the control rule acts on, and the average of the smoothed series over the full time series is the B~MSY~ proxy. 2020 carries no observation because the survey was cancelled; the random-effects model supplies a value for it, which is why the average is taken over the smoothed series rather than the observations."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/rema_tier_4_ssc.png")
```

```{r tier4-status-series, echo=FALSE, out.width="88%", fig.cap="Tier 4 stock status (biomass relative to the B~MSY~ proxy) computed on the raw survey series for the two large-male currencies. The red line is the closure threshold beta, below which the OFL is zero; the green line is half the proxy, the minimum stock size threshold. The series is shown on the raw observations rather than the smoothed fit, so it is more variable than the status reported for the specification, which is computed from the REMA fit in Figure \\@ref(fig:rema-fit)."}
knitr::include_graphics("plots/tier4_status.png")
```

```{r mmbfits, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Model fits to the observed mature biomass at survey (1,000 t), for the five models fitted under GMACS 2.20.34. Model 25.3, which was fitted under GMACS 2.20.22 to a survey series ending in 2025, is not plotted. [[author: the chunk has excluded this model since the May cycle; confirm that is still intended and that this is the reason.]]"}

# --- 1. Process Prediction Data and Add Hybrid Status ---
dfrIndxFit_plot <- wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Index_fit_summary") |> 
  dplyr::filter(case != "25.1 gmacs" & maturity != "immature") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    across(c(year, obs, base_CV, actual_CV, q, prd, prsn_res), as.numeric)
  ) |> 
  dplyr::rename(
    predicted = prd,
    residuals = prsn_res,
    model     = case
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Categorize models based on the long label *before* shortening it
    hybrid_status = ifelse(grepl("hyb_surv|hyb_both", model, ignore.case = TRUE),
                           "Hybrid Included",
                           "Standard Survey"),
    maturity_status = ifelse(grepl("new_mat", model, ignore.case = TRUE),
                           "New maturity",
                           "Old maturity"),
    # Compact shortname for the legend
    model = to_short(model),
    # Confidence interval calculations
    sd_log = sqrt(log(1 + actual_CV^2)),
    lba    = qlnorm(0.05, log(obs), sd_log),
    uba    = qlnorm(0.95, log(obs), sd_log)
  )

check <- dfrIndxFit_plot %>%
  filter(year == 2019 & sex == "male") %>%
  select(sex, hybrid_status, maturity_status, obs, model)

# --- 2. Extract Unique Observations ---
# This ensures we only plot a single set of points and black error bars
dfrObs <- dfrIndxFit_plot |> 
  dplyr::distinct(year, sex, hybrid_status, maturity_status, obs, lba, uba)

# --- 3. Generate the 4-Panel Plot ---
p_idx_final <- ggplot() +
  # Model Predictions (Colored lines, plotted first so they sit behind points)
  geom_line(
    data = dfrIndxFit_plot, 
    aes(x = year, y = predicted, color = model), 
    lwd = 0.9, 
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  # Observations (Single black error bar per year/sex/panel)
  geom_errorbar(
    data = dfrObs,
    aes(x = year, ymin = lba, ymax = uba), 
    width = 0.3, 
    color = "black",
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  # Observations (Single black point per year/sex/panel)
  geom_point(
    data = dfrObs,
    aes(x = year, y = obs), 
    size = 1.2,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  # Formatting and Scales
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(
    x = "Year", 
    y = "NMFS Survey Biomass (1,000 t)",
    color = "Model Prediction",
    subtitle = "Points/Bars: Shared Observations | Lines: Model Fits",
    caption = "Error bars represent 95% log-normal confidence intervals on observations."
  ) +
  facet_grid(sex ~ hybrid_status + maturity_status, scales = "free_y") + 
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )

print(p_idx_final)

as a convergence fix. Index_fit_summary now contains only maturity == "mature",
so the filter returns zero rows and the chunk died with "Faceting variables must
have at least one value".

Nothing cross-references fig:immfits, so disabling it leaves no dangling link.
Kept as code rather than deleted, in case an immature index returns.

[[author: delete outright if the immature index is not coming back.]]
-->
```{r immfits, eval=FALSE, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Model fits to the observed immature survey biomass for models that include the immature survey index. Panels separate models by maturity workflow (old vs. new) and hybrid treatment."}

# --- 1. Process Immature Index Data and Add Hybrid / Maturity Status ---
dfrImmFit_plot <- wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Index_fit_summary") |>
  dplyr::filter(case != "25.1 gmacs" & maturity == "immature") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    across(c(year, obs, base_CV, actual_CV, q, prd, prsn_res), as.numeric)
  ) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    predicted = prd,
    residuals = prsn_res,
    model     = case
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    hybrid_status = ifelse(grepl("hyb_surv|hyb_both", model, ignore.case = TRUE),
                           "Hybrid Included",
                           "Standard Survey"),
    maturity_status = ifelse(grepl("new_mat", model, ignore.case = TRUE),
                           "New maturity",
                           "Old maturity"),
    model = to_short(model),
    sd_log = sqrt(log(1 + actual_CV^2)),
    lba    = qlnorm(0.05, log(obs), sd_log),
    uba    = qlnorm(0.95, log(obs), sd_log)
  )

# --- 2. Extract Unique Observations ---
dfrObs <- dfrImmFit_plot |>
  dplyr::distinct(year, sex, hybrid_status, maturity_status, obs, lba, uba)

# --- 3. Generate the Plot ---
p_imm_final <- dfrImmFit_plot %>% 
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    aes(x = year, y = predicted, color = model),
    lwd = 0.9,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x = year, ymin = lba, ymax = uba),
    width = 0.3,
    color = "black",
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(x = year, y = obs),
    size = 1.2,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "NMFS Immature Survey Biomass (1,000 t)",
    color = "Model Prediction",
    subtitle = "Points/Bars: Shared Observations | Lines: Model Fits",
    caption = "Error bars represent 95% log-normal confidence intervals on observations."
  ) +
  facet_grid(sex ~ hybrid_status + maturity_status, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )

print(p_imm_final)

```

```{r catchfits, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F, fig.width=8, fig.height=8, fig.cap="Model fits to catch data (1,000 t), for all models presented."}

# --- 1. Process Catch Fit Data and Add Hybrid Status ---
dfrCatFit_plot <- wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Catch_fit_summary") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Ensure numeric types
    across(c(year, obs, cv, effort, HM, prd, rsd), as.numeric)
  ) |> 
  dplyr::rename(
    predicted = prd,
    residuals = rsd,
    model     = case
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Identify if a model includes hybrid discards based on its long name
    hybrid_status = ifelse(grepl("hyb_both|hyb_fishery", model, ignore.case = TRUE),
                           "Hybrid Included",
                           "Standard Data"),
    # Compact shortname for the legend
    model = to_short(model),
    # Create descriptive row labels for faceting
    series = dplyr::case_when(
      fleet == "Trawl_Bycatch" ~ "Non-directed Bycatch",
      type == "retained" ~ "Directed Retained (Male)",
      type == "discard" & sex == "male"   ~ "Directed Discard (Male)",
      type == "discard" & sex == "female" ~ "Directed Discard (Female)",
      TRUE ~ paste(fleet, type, sex)
    )
  )

# --- 2. Extract Unique Observations ---
# This ensures that for models sharing the same data, only one point is plotted
dfrObs <- dfrCatFit_plot |> 
  dplyr::distinct(year, series, hybrid_status, obs)

# --- 3. Generate the 2-Column Comparison Plot ---
p_catch <- ggplot() +
  # 1. Model Predictions (Lines)
  geom_line(
    data = dfrCatFit_plot, 
    aes(x = year, y = predicted, color = model), 
    lwd = 0.8, 
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  # 2. Observations (Points)
  geom_point(
    data = dfrObs,
    aes(x = year, y = obs), 
    size = 1.2,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  # 3. Formatting and Scales
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(
    x = "Year", 
    y = "Catch (1,000 t)",
    color = "Model Scenario",
    title = "Fishery Catch and Bycatch Fits",
    subtitle = "Black points: Observations | Colored lines: Model predictions",
    caption = "Observations in the 'Hybrid Included' column contain hybrid crab discards (1,000 t). [[author: the hybrid cases are not in the September model set; drop this panel or label it as a May-cycle record.]]"
  ) +
  # Grid: Series (Rows) x Hybrid Status (Columns)
  facet_grid(series ~ hybrid_status, scales = "free_y") + 
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.title=element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text.y = element_text(size = 8, angle = 0), # Keep labels readable
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )

print(p_catch)

```{r obs-101-vs-pred, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F, out.width="100%", fig.width=6.5, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Estimated abundance of male crab >101mm carapace width from the survey (black line and dots with gray 95% CI) and from each model in the assessment (colored lines). [[author: the plotted quantity is the crabpack ABUNDANCE field divided by 1,000; state the resulting unit (thousands or millions of crab) -- it could not be established from the source.]]"}
EBSdata	<-read.csv("data/survey/survey_large_male_index_derived.csv")
EBSdata	<-EBSdata[EBSdata$CATEGORY=="preferred_male",]
#==make upper and lower CIs
EBSdata$upper_bio_ci<-exp(log(EBSdata$BIOMASS_MT)+1.96*(sqrt(log(1+EBSdata$BIOMASS_MT_CV^2))))
EBSdata$lower_bio_ci<-exp(log(EBSdata$BIOMASS_MT)-1.96*(sqrt(log(1+EBSdata$BIOMASS_MT_CV^2))))
EBSdata$upper_abn_ci<-exp(log(EBSdata$ABUNDANCE)+1.96*(sqrt(log(1+EBSdata$ABUNDANCE_CV^2))))
EBSdata$lower_abn_ci<-exp(log(EBSdata$ABUNDANCE)-1.96*(sqrt(log(1+EBSdata$ABUNDANCE_CV^2))))

#==take predicted survey
dfrN_YXMSZ = wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst,"N_YXMSZ") |> 
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols=!c(case,year,sex,maturity,shell_con),
                      names_to="size",
                      values_to="est") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(year,size,est),
                              as.numeric),
                xm=paste(maturity,sex)
  );

pred_101_n2<-filter(dfrN_YXMSZ,sex=='male'&size>101)%>%
  group_by(year,case)%>%
  dplyr::summarize(ABN=sum(est))

pred_101_n3<-filter(dfrN_YXMSZ,sex=='male'&size==97.5)%>%
  group_by(year,case)%>%
  dplyr::summarize(ABN=3/5*sum(est))

pred_101_n2$tot_ABN<-(pred_101_n2$ABN+pred_101_n3$ABN)

# Shortnames for the color legend
pred_101_n2$case <- to_short(pred_101_n2$case)


male_101<-EBSdata
div_n<-1000
large_males2<-ggplot()+
  geom_ribbon(data=male_101,aes(x=YEAR,ymin=lower_abn_ci/div_n,ymax=upper_abn_ci /div_n),fill='light grey')+
  geom_line(data=male_101,aes(x=YEAR,y=ABUNDANCE/div_n))+
  geom_point(data=male_101,aes(x=YEAR,y=ABUNDANCE/div_n))+
  geom_line(data=pred_101_n2,aes(x=year,y=tot_ABN,color=case),lwd=1.1,alpha=0.6)+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position='bottom',
    legend.title=element_blank())+
  expand_limits(y=0)+
  xlab("")+
  scale_y_continuous(name="Abundance (1,0000,000s)",position='left',limits=c(0,650000))

print(large_males2)

# Weight-at-size for mature males (kg per crab) from the report model.
# Weight-at-size is fixed input data, so a single year is representative.
wt_row <- reslst$repsLst[[names(report_model)]]$IndivWeightByXM |>
  dplyr::filter(Sex == "male", Year == 1982, Maturity == "mature")
male_wt_lookup <- data.frame(

  dplyr::left_join(male_wt_lookup, by = "size") |>
  dplyr::group_by(year, case) |>
  dplyr::summarize(BIO = sum(est * wt), .groups = "drop")

pred_101_b3 <- filter(dfrN_YXMSZ, sex == 'male' & size == 97.5) |>
  dplyr::left_join(male_wt_lookup, by = "size") |>
  dplyr::group_by(year, case) |>
  dplyr::summarize(BIO = 3/5 * sum(est * wt), .groups = "drop")

  expand_limits(y = 0) +

  scale_y_continuous(name = "Biomass (1,000 mt)", position = 'left')

print(large_males_bio)

```{r predfmort, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F, fig.height=8, fig.width=8, fig.cap="Estimated fishing mortalities (per year) for the directed and non-directed fisheries."}

# --- 1. Robust Data Extraction across Models ---
# We loop through all models in reslst to find the correctly named F-dataframe
dfrF_plot <- names(reslst$repsLst) |> 
  purrr::map_dfr(function(c_name) {
    rep_obj <- reslst$repsLst[[c_name]]
    
    # Identify which name this specific model run used
    f_df_name <- intersect(
      names(rep_obj), 
      c("Fully-selected_capture_rate_by_season_sex_and_fishery", 
        "Fully-selected_FM_by_season_sex_and_fishery")
    )[1]
    
    if (is.na(f_df_name)) return(NULL)
    
    # Extract and clean
    rep_obj[[f_df_name]] |> 
      dplyr::mutate(
        Model = c_name,
        # Ensure consistency across versions (some use 'year', others 'Year')
        Year = as.numeric(year)
      )
  })

# --- 2. Clean and Filter Data for Plotting ---
plot_dat <- dfrF_plot |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Rename fleets for the report
    Fleet = dplyr::case_when(
      fleet == "Pot_Fishery" ~ "Directed Pot Fishery",
      fleet == "Trawl_Bycatch" ~ "Non-directed Bycatch",
      TRUE ~ fleet
    ),
    # Capitalize sex for headers
    Sex = stringr::str_to_title(sex),
    # Ensure mortality values are numeric (assuming season 2 is the primary fishery)
    F_value = as.numeric(`2`),
    # Compact shortname for the legend
    Model   = to_short(Model)
  ) |>
  # Filter only for the primary fishing fleets
  dplyr::filter(Fleet %in% c("Directed Pot Fishery", "Non-directed Bycatch"))

# --- 3. Generate the Comparison Plot ---
p_f_mort <- ggplot(plot_dat, aes(x = Year, y = F_value, color = Model, group = Model)) +
  # Model estimates
  geom_line(lwd = 1.1, alpha = 0.7) +
  # Layout and Scales
  facet_grid(Fleet ~ Sex, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Estimated Fully-Selected Fishing Mortality",
    subtitle = "Calculated for the primary fishing season (Season 2)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Fishing Mortality (F)",
    color = element_blank()
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )

print(p_f_mort)

```{r predmat, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F, fig.height=8, fig.width=6.5, fig.cap="Estimated (black line) or specified (colored lines) probabilities of maturing."}
# --- 1. Extract and Process Maturity Data ---
# case_for_data_table can be a single string or a vector of strings
plotdat_all <- case_for_mat_plot %>%
  purrr::map_dfr(function(case_name) {
    # Access the output list directly
    dat <- reslst$outsLst[[case_name]]$mature_probability
    
    if (is.null(dat)) {
      message("Warning: No mature_probability data for ", case_name)
      return(NULL)
    }
    
    # Pivot from wide to long format
    dat %>%
      tidyr::pivot_longer(
        cols = -c(Sex, Year),
        names_to = "width",
        values_to = "prob"
      ) %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        # Compact shortname for the legend
        Model = as.character(to_short(case_name)),
        # Logic to separate models with "newmat" (uses long label for the test)
        Maturity_Source = ifelse(grepl("new_mat", case_name, ignore.case = TRUE),
                                 "New Maturity Workflow",
                                 "Standard Maturity Data"),
        width = as.numeric(as.character(width)),
        prob = as.numeric(prob),
        # Ensure Year is a factor for discrete coloring if desired,
        # or keep numeric for a gradient
        Year_Fact = as.factor(Year)
      )
  })

# --- 2. Generate the Split Plot ---
p_molt <- plotdat_all %>%
  mutate(Year = as.numeric(Year)) %>%
 ggplot(aes(x = width, y = prob, color = Year_Fact)) +
  # Use group to ensure lines are drawn per Year/Model combination
  geom_line(lwd = 1.1, alpha = 0.7) +
  # Force y-axis from 0 to 1
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "Carapace Width (mm)", 
    y = "Probability of Terminal Molt",
    col = "Year",
    title = "Probability of Maturing / Terminal Molt",
    subtitle = "Separated by Maturity Data Specification"
  ) +
  # Facet rows by Data Source (Standard vs Newmat) and columns by Sex
  facet_grid(Maturity_Source ~ Sex) + 
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )

# Render the plot
print(p_molt)

```{r nat-m, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F, fig.height=7.5, fig.width=6.5, fig.cap="Estimated natural mortality (per year) by sex and maturity state. Natural mortality in all years previous to 2018 and after 2019 are equal to the estimated M in 2017. Note that the y-axis is capped at 5."}


# --- 1. Extract and Process Natural Mortality Data ---
dfrMbyXM_plot <- wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Natural_mortality-by-class") |> 
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(case, year, sex, maturity),
    names_to = "size", 
    values_to = "M_value"
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    size = as.numeric(size),
    M_value = as.numeric(M_value)
  ) |> 
  # Filter for selected models and the base size class
  # (M is typically constant across sizes in these models)
  dplyr::filter(size == 27.5) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Clean up labels for the report
    Sex = stringr::str_to_title(sex),
    Maturity = stringr::str_to_title(maturity),
    # Compact shortname for the legend
    Model = to_short(case)
  )

# --- 2. Generate the Comparison Plot ---
p_nat_m <- ggplot(dfrMbyXM_plot, aes(x = year, y = M_value, color = Model, group = Model)) +
  # Model Estimates
  geom_line(lwd = 1.1, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  # Focus on the 2018-2019 mortality event window; allow the immature-index
  # model's elevated mature-male M to be visible (let ggplot pick the upper
  # limit from the data rather than clipping at 5).
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2015, 2022)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Estimated Natural Mortality (M)",
    subtitle = "Focusing on 2018-2019 Mortality Events",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Natural Mortality (M)",
    color = element_blank()
  ) +
  ylim(0, 5) +
  # 2x2 grid by Sex and Maturity
  facet_wrap(~Sex + Maturity) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )

# Render the plot

# Size composition fits

```{r size-comp-plots, results='asis', echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, out.width="100%"}

# Order comp plots by base fleet, comp_type, sex, maturity so that fits across
# model variants (hybrid/compfix/plus_group; new vs. old maturity ogive) for
# the same data block sit next to each other.
img_folder <- "plots"
img_files  <- list.files(path = img_folder, pattern = "^size_comp_plot_", full.names = TRUE)

parse_meta <- function(f) {
  base  <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(f))
  desc  <- sub("^size_comp_plot_\\d+_", "", base)
  parts <- strsplit(desc, "_")[[1]]
  sex_idx <- which(parts %in% c("male", "female"))[1]
  if (is.na(sex_idx)) {
    return(data.frame(file = f, fleet_full = NA_character_, base_fleet = NA_character_,
                      comp_type = NA_character_, sex = NA_character_,
                      maturity = NA_character_, ogive = NA_character_,
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
  }
  fleet_full <- paste(parts[seq_len(sex_idx - 1)], collapse = "_")
  sex        <- parts[sex_idx]
  comp_type  <- parts[sex_idx + 1]
  maturity   <- parts[sex_idx + 2]
  ogive      <- if (sex_idx + 3 <= length(parts))
                  paste(parts[seq(sex_idx + 3, length(parts))], collapse = "_") else NA_character_
  base_fleet <- tolower(fleet_full)
  base_fleet <- sub("_(hybrid|compfix|plus_group)$", "", base_fleet)
  data.frame(file = f, fleet_full = fleet_full, base_fleet = base_fleet,
             comp_type = comp_type, sex = sex, maturity = maturity, ogive = ogive,
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

meta <- do.call(rbind, lapply(img_files, parse_meta))

meta$comp_type <- factor(meta$comp_type, levels = c("retained", "total", "discarded"))
meta$sex       <- factor(meta$sex,       levels = c("female", "male"))
meta$maturity  <- factor(meta$maturity,  levels = c("immature", "mature", "undetermined"))

meta <- meta[order(meta$base_fleet, meta$comp_type, meta$sex, meta$maturity,
                   meta$fleet_full, meta$ogive), ]

make_caption <- function(f) {
  base <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(f))
  desc <- sub("^size_comp_plot_\\d+_", "", base)
  desc <- gsub("_", " ", desc)
  # "compfix" and "plus group" are internal configuration shorthands from the
  # fleet-splitting in the setup chunk; they read as if they were separate
  # fleets. Name what they mean, and say which models are plotted -- the caption
  # previously identified the panel only by maturity workflow (2026-08-29).
  desc <- sub("Pot fishery compfix", "Pot Fishery (corrected composition)", desc)
  desc <- sub("Pot fishery plus group", "Pot Fishery (expanded plus group)", desc)
  desc <- sub("NMFS Trawl", "NMFS trawl survey", desc)
  paste0("Model fits (lines) to size composition data (grey bars), all models ",
         "presented: ", desc, ". Proportions by 5 mm carapace-width bin.")
}

# Initialize trackers with empty strings
last_fleet <- ""
last_sex_mat <- ""

for (i in 1:nrow(meta)) {
  row <- meta[i, ]
  
  # 1. Check for Fleet change (## Header)
  if (row$base_fleet != last_fleet) {
    # Print the header (cleaning up underscores for readability)
    cat("\n## Fleet: ", tools::toTitleCase(gsub("_", " ", row$base_fleet)), "\n\n")
    
    # Update tracker
    last_fleet <- row$base_fleet
    # Reset sex_mat tracker so it prints for the new fleet section 
    # even if it's the same category as the end of the last fleet
    last_sex_mat <- "" 
  }
  
  # 2. Check for Sex/Maturity change (### Header)
  current_sex_mat <- paste(row$sex, "and", row$maturity)
  if (current_sex_mat != last_sex_mat) {
    cat("\n### ", tools::toTitleCase(current_sex_mat), "\n\n")
    last_sex_mat <- current_sex_mat
  }
  
  # 3. Print the Plot
  # {width=100%} is required. These are raw markdown images emitted with cat(),
  # so the chunk's out.width does NOT apply to them -- knitr only sizes figures
  # it generates itself. The size-comp PNGs are 8 x 8 in at 300 dpi against a
  # 6.5 in text width, so without this they ran off the page (2026-08-29).
  cat("![", make_caption(row$file), "](", URLencode(row$file), "){width=100%}\n\n", sep = "")
  
  # Optional: Add page break after every plot, or move this inside the header 
  # logic if you only want page breaks between fleets.
  cat("\\newpage\n\n")
}

# Appendix C. Convergence diagnostics

```{r conv-appendix-setup, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
## Appendix C reads the PER-MODEL jitter files. 05_run_jitter.R writes
## Models/rda_jitter.RData at a fixed path whatever --model is given, so each run
## overwrites the last; the per-model copies below are what survives. Absent
## files drop out with a visible note rather than a plausible blank row.
##
## Only WITHIN-model statistics are tabulated -- how often a model finds its own
## best optimum. Likelihoods are NOT compared across these rows: two of the three
## experiments run on forked TPLs whose objective functions carry terms stock
## 2.20.34 does not have (see diagnostic_models in 0-models.R).
conv_files <- c(
  "Model 26.1b (accepted)" = "Models/rda_jitter.RData",
  "Model 26.2 (male-only)" = "Models/rda_jitter_male_only.RData",
  "Model 26.1c (2019 data)" = "Models/rda_jitter_data2019.RData",
  "Model 26.1 (2025 base)"  = "Models/rda_jitter_25.2c.RData",
  "26.d1 stability"         = "Models/rda_jitter_stability.RData",
  "26.d3 eqmdevs"           = "Models/rda_jitter_eqmdevs.RData",
  "26.d4 combined"          = "Models/rda_jitter_combined.RData",
  "26.d5 male-only+eqmdevs" = "Models/rda_jitter_male_only_eqmdevs.RData"
)

conv_row <- function(lab, path) {
  if (!file.exists(path)) return(NULL)
  e <- new.env(); load(path, envir = e); j <- e$jitter
  sm <- j$summary; rs <- j$results
  ok <- !is.na(rs$mode)                       # runs that reached an optimum
  ## The recovery rate that matters is for the model's OWN BEST fit, which is not
  ## what pct_at_best_mode reports. classify_modes() (R/gmacs_jitter.R:604) orders
  ## clusters by their MINIMUM nll and letters them A, B, C best-first, but only
  ## once a cluster holds >= 3 runs; smaller ones are bucketed "minor" whatever
  ## their likelihood. So mode A is the best LETTERED cluster, not the best
  ## solution found: when the true best fit is reached by one or two runs it is
  ## bucketed minor and A is a worse optimum entirely. That is the accepted
  ## model's case exactly. Computed directly here for every model.
  best <- min(rs$objFun[ok], na.rm = TRUE)
  n_at_best <- sum(abs(rs$objFun[ok] - best) < 0.01)
  nmodes <- length(setdiff(unique(rs$mode[ok]), "minor"))
  ## OFL spread across NEAR-OPTIMAL runs (within 2 nll of the best), not across
  ## all usable ones. The all-runs spread answers "how bad can a converged but
  ## wrong run be", which is not the question here and inverts the ranking: on
  ## all usable runs the male-only model looks the WORST of the four despite
  ## having by far the best recovery rate, because its poor runs are further
  ## away. Conditioning on near-optimal runs asks how much the OFL moves among
  ## solutions the data cannot separate, which is the management-relevant spread.
  near <- ok & (rs$objFun - best) <= 2
  n_near <- sum(near)
  ofl_sp <- if (n_near > 1)
    100 * (max(rs$ofl_tot[near]) - min(rs$ofl_tot[near])) / min(rs$ofl_tot[near]) else NA_real_
  data.frame(
    Model = lab,
    Converged = sprintf("%d/%d", sm$n_converged[1], sm$n_runs[1]),
    `Meets 1e-3` = sprintf("%d/%d", sm$n_meets_conventional[1], sm$n_runs[1]),
    Optima = nmodes,
    `Best fit found` = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", n_at_best, 100 * n_at_best / sum(ok)),
    `Best lettered mode` = sprintf("%.1f%%", sm$pct_at_best_mode[1]),
    `OFL spread, near-optimal` = if (is.na(ofl_sp)) sprintf("- (n=%d)", n_near)
                                 else sprintf("%.1f%% (n=%d)", ofl_sp, n_near),
    `nll span` = sprintf("%.1f", diff(range(rs$objFun[ok], na.rm = TRUE))),
    check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

conv_tab <- do.call(rbind, Map(conv_row, names(conv_files), conv_files))

## Statistics quoted in the concluding paragraph. Computed, not written down:
## three of the review findings on this appendix were hardcoded literals that had
## gone stale against a re-promoted fit, and this paragraph is its most quoted.
.rate <- function(path) {
  if (!file.exists(path)) return(c(NA, NA))
  e <- new.env(); load(path, envir = e); rs <- e$jitter$results
  ok <- !is.na(rs$mode); best <- min(rs$objFun[ok], na.rm = TRUE)
  c(sum(abs(rs$objFun[ok] - best) < 0.01), sum(ok))
}
.r_acc <- .rate(conv_files[["Model 26.1b (accepted)"]])
## Recovery rates are reported as counts with a confidence interval. A formal
## test of proportions was drafted here and removed (Grant, 2026-08-30): the
## p-value is not the register this document is read in, and the interval makes
## the same point -- where two intervals overlap heavily, 100 runs cannot
## separate the configurations.
.ci <- function(path) {
  r <- .rate(path)
  if (anyNA(r)) return(c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
  100 * stats::binom.test(r[1], r[2])$conf.int[1:2]
}
cv_pct_acc  <- 100 * .r_acc[1] / .r_acc[2]
cv_ci_hi    <- 100 * stats::binom.test(.r_acc[1], .r_acc[2])$conf.int[2]
cv_n_acc    <- .r_acc[2]
.r_eqm  <- .rate(conv_files[["26.d3 eqmdevs"]])
.r_stab <- .rate(conv_files[["26.d1 stability"]])
.r_mo   <- .rate(conv_files[["Model 26.2 (male-only)"]])
cv_pct_eqm  <- 100 * .r_eqm[1] / .r_eqm[2]
cv_pct_stab <- 100 * .r_stab[1] / .r_stab[2]
cv_pct_mo   <- 100 * .r_mo[1] / .r_mo[2]
## 26.d5 is the one configuration that improved on the model it was built from,
## so it is tested against 26.2 rather than against the accepted two-sex model.
.r_d5 <- .rate(conv_files[["26.d5 male-only+eqmdevs"]])
.r_d4 <- .rate(conv_files[["26.d4 combined"]])
cv_pct_d5  <- 100 * .r_d5[1] / .r_d5[2]
cv_pct_d4  <- 100 * .r_d4[1] / .r_d4[2]
cv_ci_d5   <- .ci(conv_files[["26.d5 male-only+eqmdevs"]])
cv_ci_mo   <- .ci(conv_files[["Model 26.2 (male-only)"]])
cv_ci_stab <- .ci(conv_files[["26.d1 stability"]])
cv_ci_eqm  <- .ci(conv_files[["26.d3 eqmdevs"]])

## Where the movement between optima actually sits, by parameter class. Written
## by 05b_jitter_movement_decomposition.R; movement is the RANGE (max - min) of
## each parameter across the retained optima, summed within class. Range rather
## than variance because these are alternative optima, not draws from a
## distribution -- one run at an extreme is as meaningful as the spread of the
## rest. Retained = converged (max|grad| < 1e-2) AND within 2 nll of the best,
## which is what keeps this a measure of the likelihood's shape near the optimum
## rather than a measure of optimiser failure.
mv_all <- Sys.glob("data/diagnostics/jitter_movement_by_class_*.csv")
## Pick the ACCEPTED model's file by name. A sort order would select it only by
## alphabetical accident and would silently switch models when another
## configuration is decomposed.
mv_path <- grep("26_gmacs_update_newmat_plus_group", mv_all, value = TRUE)
mv_have <- length(mv_path) == 1
if (mv_have) {
  mv <- read.csv(mv_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  mv <- mv[order(-mv$share_pct), ]
  ## Shares are recomputed from total_range rather than read, so a hand-edited
  ## share_pct column cannot reach the page.
  mv$share_pct <- 100 * mv$total_range / sum(mv$total_range)
  stopifnot("movement shares must sum to 100" = abs(sum(mv$share_pct) - 100) < 1e-6)
  .sh <- function(cl) sum(mv$share_pct[mv$class %in% cl])
  mv_sexalloc <- .sh("sex allocation")
  mv_female   <- .sh(c("female", "female (F offsets)"))
  mv_male     <- .sh("male")
  mv_fem_plus <- mv_sexalloc + mv_female
  mv_n_opt    <- mv$n_optima[1]
  mv_npar_m   <- mv$n_parameters[mv$class == "male"]
  mv_npar_sa  <- mv$n_parameters[mv$class == "sex allocation"]
  ## Movement PER PARAMETER. The raw counts invite a misleading comparison --
  ## "female" is split across two classes, so male (101) exceeds the female class
  ## (91) but not the female classes combined (134). Density avoids the question
  ## and is the sharper statement anyway.
  .dens <- function(cl) sum(mv$total_range[mv$class %in% cl]) / sum(mv$n_parameters[mv$class %in% cl])
  mv_dens_sa   <- .dens("sex allocation")
  mv_dens_male <- .dens("male")
  mv_dens_ratio <- mv_dens_sa / mv_dens_male
} else {
  mv_sexalloc <- mv_female <- mv_male <- mv_fem_plus <- NA_real_
  mv_dens_sa <- mv_dens_male <- mv_dens_ratio <- NA_real_
  mv_npar_m <- mv_npar_sa <- mv_n_opt <- NA_integer_
}

## Cross-model comparison. Shares are the safe currency here: movement is a RANGE
## across retained optima, and range is not independent of how many optima were
## retained (40 / 20 / 31 across these models), so absolute totals carry a caveat
## that shares do not. `26.d1 stability` is absent by necessity, not oversight --
## only 2 of its runs land within 2 nll of its best fit, below the 3 the
## decomposition needs, because its optima are too dispersed to form a cluster.
.mv_lab <- c("26_gmacs_update_newmat_plus_group" = "Model 26.1b (accepted)",
             "26_gmacs_eqmdevs"                  = "26.d3 eqmdevs",
             "26_gmacs_male_only"                = "Model 26.2 (male-only)",
             "26_gmacs_male_only_eqmdevs"        = "26.d5 male-only + eqmdevs")
## Restrict to the configurations this appendix actually discusses. Decomposition
## files for other models appear in data/diagnostics/ as the diagnostic work
## continues; a new one must not silently join the table (nor abort the knit, as
## it did on 2026-08-30 when a male_only_eqmdevs file landed mid-session). An
## unrecognised file is reported in the console and skipped.
.mv_known <- Filter(function(f) {
  m <- read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)$model[1]
  ok <- m %in% names(.mv_lab)
  if (!ok) message("conv-appendix: skipping unlisted decomposition for '", m, "'")
  ok
}, mv_all)
xm_have <- length(.mv_known) > 1
if (xm_have) {
  xm <- do.call(rbind, lapply(.mv_known, function(f) {
    d <- read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    tot <- sum(d$total_range)
    cls <- function(cl) sum(d$total_range[d$class %in% cl])
    data.frame(
      Model = unname(.mv_lab[d$model[1]]),
      Optima = d$n_optima[1],
      `Total movement` = tot,
      `Sex allocation (%)` = 100 * cls("sex allocation") / tot,
      `Female + sex allocation (%)` = 100 * cls(c("female", "female (F offsets)", "sex allocation")) / tot,
      `Male (%)` = 100 * cls("male") / tot,
      `Male movement` = cls("male"),
      check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }))
  xm <- xm[order(-xm$`Total movement`), ]
  stopifnot("a cross-model row lost its label" = !any(is.na(xm$Model)))
  ## Plain-named scalars for the prose. Inline `r ` code cannot carry
  ## backtick-quoted column names, so pull them out here.
  .xg <- function(col, mdl) xm[[col]][xm$Model == mdl]
  xm_male_acc  <- .xg("Male movement", "Model 26.1b (accepted)")
  xm_male_eqm  <- .xg("Male movement", "26.d3 eqmdevs")
  xm_male_pct_eqm <- .xg("Male (%)", "26.d3 eqmdevs")
  xm_sa_eqm    <- .xg("Sex allocation (%)", "26.d3 eqmdevs")
  xm_fp_eqm    <- .xg("Female + sex allocation (%)", "26.d3 eqmdevs")
  xm_tot_acc   <- .xg("Total movement", "Model 26.1b (accepted)")
  xm_tot_male  <- .xg("Total movement", "Model 26.2 (male-only)")
  xm_optima_lab <- paste(xm$Optima, collapse = ", ")   # table row order, not sorted
} else {
  xm_male_acc <- xm_male_eqm <- xm_sa_eqm <- xm_fp_eqm <- NA_real_
  xm_tot_acc <- xm_tot_male <- NA_real_; xm_optima_lab <- "NA"
}
conv_have <- !is.null(conv_tab) && nrow(conv_tab) > 0
if (conv_have) stopifnot(
  "a convergence row lost its model label" = !any(is.na(conv_tab$Model)))
```

The June 2026 SSC asked that a focused convergence section identify which parameters separate the jitter clouds. This appendix collects the jitter evidence for every model jittered this cycle, together with three structural experiments built specifically to diagnose the multimodality. **None of the three is an assessment model and none is proposed for any purpose other than diagnosis** --- they are registered separately from the model set in `0-models.R` for that reason.

The diagnostic identified three independent pathologies in the accepted model:

1. `M_pars_est[15]`, the 2019 immature-female natural mortality deviation, is structurally non-identified. It is the only one of the 412 parameters that moves while the objective function does not.
2. The recruitment sex ratio is carried by 44 logits bounded at plus or minus 100 whose only effective restraint is a standard deviation of 2.0 hardcoded in the source rather than read from the control file. Thirteen of the 44 are estimated beyond two standard deviations of that penalty. They are nowhere near the plus or minus 100 bounds --- the estimates span -3.6 to +4.2 --- so it is the penalty, not the bound, that is failing to restrain them.
3. The 1982 initial numbers at length are 83 parameters whose overall level is entirely unpenalised. The only term touching them is a first-difference smoothness penalty, and first differences are invariant to shifting a whole group.

The attribution analysis points at the same place. Of the parameters that most separate the jitter clouds (Table \@ref(tab:jitter-attribution)), the single largest separator is `logit_rec_prop_est`, the recruitment sex allocation --- that is, the second pathology above is not merely present in the model, it is the leading explanation for which optimum a run lands in. That is the direct answer to the SSC's question, and it is also the reason the male-only simplification, which removes the sex allocation entirely, is the only configuration in Table \@ref(tab:conv-table) that reliably recovers its own best fit.

Decomposing the movement between optima by parameter class puts a number on that (Table \@ref(tab:movement-table)). Across the `r mv_n_opt` near-equivalent optima, the recruitment sex allocation alone accounts for `r .f(mv_sexalloc, 1)` percent of all parameter movement, and the female and sex-allocation parameters together account for `r .f(mv_fem_plus, 1)` percent. The male parameters account for `r .f(mv_male, 1)` percent across `r mv_npar_m` parameters, where the sex allocation reaches `r .f(mv_sexalloc, 1)` percent on just `r mv_npar_sa` --- about `r .f(mv_dens_ratio, 0)` times as much movement per parameter. The alternative optima this model admits are therefore very largely disagreements about the female population and how recruitment is split between the sexes, rather than about the male population the assessment exists to manage. That is the clearest quantitative case for the male-only direction, and it is measured on the accepted model itself rather than inferred from the sensitivity.

Running the same decomposition on the experiments turns that association into a mechanism (Table \@ref(tab:xmodel-table)). The equilibrium backbone in `26.d3 eqmdevs` did what it was built to do and nothing else: the male parameters' share of movement fell from `r .f(mv_male, 1)` to `r .f(xm_male_pct_eqm, 1)` percent, because anchoring the 1982 structure removes the freedom that had been propagating through the male side. But it does not touch the sex ratio, and sex-allocation movement barely moved. Its *share* therefore rose, from `r .f(mv_sexalloc, 1)` to `r .f(xm_sa_eqm, 1)` percent, and the female-and-sex-allocation total from `r .f(mv_fem_plus, 1)` to `r .f(xm_fp_eqm, 1)` percent. Fixing the initialisation made the sex allocation *more* dominant, not less, which is a sufficient explanation for why it did not improve the recovery rate.

`Model 26.2` removes the sex allocation altogether, and total movement collapses from `r .f(xm_tot_acc, 1)` to `r .f(xm_tot_male, 2)`, with what remains dominated by the shared recruitment deviations. So the male-only model's advantage is not that it has fewer parameters in the abstract; it is that the parameters carrying almost all of the movement between optima are precisely the ones it deletes. Two qualifications belong with this. The absolute movement totals are ranges taken across different numbers of retained optima --- `r xm_optima_lab` for the three models --- and a range is not independent of how many runs enter it, so the totals should be read as indicative while the shares, which are unaffected, carry the argument. And `26.d1 stability` cannot appear in this table at all: only two of its runs land within two likelihood units of its best fit, fewer than the decomposition requires, because its optima are too dispersed to form a cluster of near-equivalent solutions. That is consistent with its likelihood span being among the widest in Table \@ref(tab:conv-table), at 311.8 against the accepted model's 301.6.

Each experiment addressed a different subset. `26.d1 stability` fixed the first two and left the third; `26.d3 eqmdevs` replaced the third with an equilibrium backbone times penalised deviations and left the first two; `26.d2 initscaled` rescaled the initial-condition parameterisation and was set aside without jittering when its fit to the data proved 138 likelihood units worse. A configuration with all three fixed at once was then built and jittered, `26.d4`, and it did not resolve the multimodality either. What did work was applying one of the fixes --- the equilibrium-backbone initialisation --- to the male-only model rather than to the two-sex one.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

```{r conv-table, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
if (conv_have) {
  flextable::flextable(conv_tab) |>
    flextable::set_table_properties(opts_pdf = list(caption_repeat = FALSE)) |>
    flextable::fontsize(size = 8, part = "all") |>
    flextable::autofit() |>
    flextable::set_caption(
      caption = paste(
        "Jitter convergence statistics, 100 runs per model. 'Best fit found' is the number of runs",
        "recovering that model's own lowest objective function. That is not the same as the best LETTERED",
        "mode: clusters are lettered in order of likelihood, best first, but only once a cluster holds at",
        "least three runs, so a best fit reached by one or two runs is bucketed as minor and the lettered",
        "figure then describes a different and worse optimum. No likelihood is tabulated because none is",
        "comparable across these rows: the models are fit to different data (different terminal years, a",
        "truncated series, males only) and two of them run on modified source. The nll span is the spread",
        "WITHIN each model.",
        "The OFL spread is taken over NEAR-OPTIMAL runs only, those within two likelihood units of each",
        "model's best fit, which is how much the OFL moves among solutions the data cannot separate. Taken",
        "over all converged runs instead it would rank the models in the opposite order, because it would",
        "then be measuring how far a wrong run can wander rather than how reproducible the answer is.",
        "Model 26.d1's entry is not meaningful: only two of its runs qualify."),
      autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "conv-table"))
} else {
  cat("*No per-model jitter files found; see `05_run_jitter.R`.*")
}
```

\elandscape


The pattern across the table is that the two-sex reconfigurations did not work and the male-only one did. The accepted model recovers its own best fit in `r .f(cv_pct_acc, 1)` percent of converged runs and `26.d3 eqmdevs` in `r .f(cv_pct_eqm, 1)` percent. Those differences, and `26.d1 stability`'s `r .f(cv_pct_stab, 1)` percent, are **too small to be resolved by 100 runs**. The 95 percent interval on the accepted model's `r .f(.r_acc[1], 0)`-in-`r cv_n_acc` rate runs from zero to about `r .f(cv_ci_hi, 0)` percent, and the intervals for `eqmdevs` (to `r .f(cv_ci_eqm[2], 0)` percent) and `stability` (to `r .f(cv_ci_stab[2], 0)` percent) sit almost entirely inside it. Separating rates of this size would take several hundred runs, not one hundred. The correct reading is therefore not that these experiments made recovery slightly worse --- the data cannot support that --- but that none of them improved it detectably. `26.d4 combined`, which applies all three fixes at once, is no better: `r .f(cv_pct_d4, 1)` percent, well inside the range the accepted model's own rate could take, and it converged less often than any other configuration. Its printed "best mode" share of 16.7 percent must not be quoted as a recovery rate --- that mode sits 5.9 likelihood units above its own best fit, which only `r .f(.r_d4[1], 0)` of `r .f(.r_d4[2], 0)` converged runs reached. So fixing all three pathologies in the two-sex model does not resolve the multimodality either.

Two configurations do stand out, and both remove the female population. `Model 26.2` recovers its best fit in `r .f(cv_pct_mo, 1)` percent of converged runs --- `r .f(.r_mo[1], 0)` runs of `r .f(.r_mo[2], 0)`, against one of `r cv_n_acc` for the accepted model, a difference far outside anything 100 runs could produce by chance. `26.d5`, which adds the equilibrium-backbone initialisation to that model, reaches `r .f(cv_pct_d5, 1)` percent, `r .f(.r_d5[1], 0)` runs of `r .f(.r_d5[2], 0)` --- the only configuration tested that improved on the model it was derived from. Its likelihood span across usable runs is `r .f(diff(range(local({e<-new.env(); load(conv_files[["26.d5 male-only+eqmdevs"]], envir=e); r<-e$jitter$results; r$objFun[!is.na(r$mode)]}))), 1)` units, where every other configuration in the table spans more than a hundred, and its promoted fit is the only one in this study to meet the 0.001 gradient criterion. Two qualifications belong with it: the 95 percent intervals on the two rates overlap --- `r .f(cv_ci_d5[1], 0)` to `r .f(cv_ci_d5[2], 0)` percent against `r .f(cv_ci_mo[1], 0)` to `r .f(cv_ci_mo[2], 0)` --- so the improvement is real on this evidence but not decisive, and rests on a single set of 100 runs; and it met the gradient criterion in only 3 runs of 100 against `Model 26.2`'s 9, so the two convergence measures disagree and both are reported. The recovery measure concerns which optimum a run finds, the gradient measure how precisely it stops.

The two ingredients are complementary rather than alternative. Removing the sex allocation removes the largest single share of the movement between optima; anchoring the initial condition removes most of what is left. Neither is sufficient alone --- the same initialisation applied to the two-sex model, `26.d3`, changed nothing detectable. What `eqmdevs` did buy is a halving of the likelihood span across runs, so a poor starting point ends up far less poor, and a penalty burden roughly halved --- real improvements in conditioning that did not translate into finding one optimum reliably. The male-only simplification is the configuration that materially improves recovery, at `r .f(cv_pct_mo, 1)` percent, and it is one of only two rows in the table where the best fit and the best lettered mode are the same solution (`Model 26.1`, the 2025 base, is the other). In the accepted model they are different solutions 0.81 likelihood units apart, and in `26.d3 eqmdevs` they differ as well --- so in those configurations a single cold start is more likely to land on a reproducible but inferior optimum than on the best one. That is why it is carried in the model set as `Model 26.2` and the three experiments here are not.

## Caveats

Three qualifications attach to the experiments above, and none of them is a detail of implementation.

**The equilibrium backbone is unfished.** `26.d3 eqmdevs` anchors the 1982 population on an *unfished* equilibrium, following the formulation it was ported from, but the eastern Bering Sea snow crab stock had been fished since the late 1970s. The effect is visible in the result: 1982 mature male biomass moves from 212.9 to 300.9 kt. Switching the backbone to a fished equilibrium is a small change to the same code, and it has not been made. This experiment should therefore not be judged finally on the results reported here.

**Several of the experiments require modified source.** `26.d1 stability`, `26.d3 eqmdevs`, `26.d4 combined` and `26.d5` were run with forked GMACS source trees rather than the stock 2.20.34 binary used for every model in the assessment. This matters most for `26.d5`, since it is the configuration these results point toward: it cannot be reproduced, or brought forward as a candidate, without the initialisation mode being merged into the released version first. `stability` changes a penalty standard deviation that is hardcoded in the source rather than read from the control file; `eqmdevs` adds an initialisation mode and a deviation penalty occupying a control-file slot that is dead code in the released version. **The results in this appendix are therefore not reproducible with the stock binary**, and the forks are recorded with the models. The shared source tree the assessment itself is built from is unmodified and is checked against its hash at every build.

**One of the fixes is a structural assumption, not a neutral correction.** Fixing the 2019 immature-female mortality deviation removes that mortality event for immature females entirely, while immature males and mature females retain theirs. It is defensible --- the parameter is not identified by the data, so estimating it is not informative either --- but it is an assumption about what happened in 2019 rather than a neutral numerical repair, and any configuration carrying it should be presented on that basis. It is not, however, the main reason the experiments move the OFL. Isolating the changes shows the equilibrium initialisation contributing more on its own than the mortality and sex-ratio fixes together, and `26.d3 eqmdevs` carries that initialisation without the mortality fix at all. The OFL movement in these experiments should be attributed to the initialisation first.
